verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Man and His Times
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth (v. 1). The word of the LORD came to him in Josiah's thirteenth year (v. 2) and kept coming through Jehoiakim and to the end of Zedekiah's eleventh year, until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month (v. 3): about forty years, ending in the ruin of the city.
verseByVerse.theology: A priest's son is given a word for a nation in its last forty years, and he must say it until the end comes.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, to whom the word of the LORD came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, and until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin,

The book begins with a name, a father and a village. Jeremiah is a priest's son from Anathoth, a small place within sight of Jerusalem. He is not a court official or a member of the temple establishment in the capital. He comes from the edge, and he will spend his life telling the centre what it does not want to hear.

to whom the word of the LORD came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

The date matters. Josiah was the last good king of Judah, the one who did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the way of David his father (2 Kgs 22:2). Jeremiah's ministry begins during a national revival. He is called in the best years, and he will watch them end.

It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, and until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month.

From Josiah's thirteenth year to the fifth month of Zedekiah's eleventh is about forty years. Forty years of preaching, and the summary of how it went is in the last phrase: until the captivity of Jerusalem. The city fell. The nation went into exile. Under Jehoiakim the empire had already closed in (2 Kgs 24:1).

Hold that together before reading a line of what follows. This is the record of a man who preached faithfully for four decades and saw his country destroyed. Judged by results, he failed. Judged by faithfulness, he is one of the great men of the Bible. Those are not the same measure, and confusing them has wrecked more ministries and more Christians than open sin has.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Before I Formed You in the Womb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, I appointed you a prophet to the nations (vv. 4-5). Jeremiah objects that he cannot speak and is only a youth (v. 6), and is told to go where he is sent and say what he is given, for I am with you to deliver you (vv. 7-8). Then the LORD touches his mouth: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth, and sets him over nations to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The call rests on God's prior choice, God's presence and God's words, not on the prophet's ability.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

The narrator's voice becomes the prophet's own. What follows is not a report about Jeremiah; it is Jeremiah telling you what happened to him.

"Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations."

Four verbs, and God is the subject of every one. He formed, he knew, he consecrated, he appointed. And all four happened before Jeremiah had done anything at all, before he had any character to commend him or any failure to disqualify him.

I knew you is more than knowing facts about him. It is the knowledge of relationship, the way a husband knows his wife. Before there was a person to know, God knew him. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them (Ps 139:16).

The same pattern is claimed by the servant of Isaiah, The LORD called me from the womb (Isa 49:1), and by Paul, who described himself as one who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace (Gal 1:15). John the Baptist was filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb (Luke 1:15).

Two things follow for anyone reading. The first is that God deals with unborn children as persons he knows, names and has purposes for. The second is pastoral: your significance is not something you are building. It was settled before you existed, by God, and no failure of yours can vote on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth."

The response is not enthusiasm. It is dismay. Ah, Lord GOD! is a cry, not a greeting. And the objection is in two parts: I cannot do this, and I am too young to be taken seriously.

Both are probably true. That is the point. Moses said the same thing at the burning bush: I am not eloquent, I am slow of speech and of tongue (Exod 4:10). God's answer to Moses was not a compliment about his hidden potential but a question: Who has made man's mouth?, and a promise: I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak (Exod 4:11-12).

Notice what God never says in these calls. He never says, you are better than you think. He says, I will be with you. Confidence for service does not come from a higher estimate of yourself; it comes from a higher estimate of God.

And youth is not a disqualification in Scripture. Paul told a young minister, Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity (1 Tim 4:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to me, "Do not say, 'I am only a youth'; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the LORD said to me, "Do not say, 'I am only a youth'; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak.

God does not argue with the objection; he forbids it: do not say it. Then he replaces the two halves of Jeremiah's excuse with two commands that put the responsibility where it belongs. Where you go is not your decision: to all to whom I send you, you shall go. What you say is not your decision either: whatever I command you, you shall speak.

That is a hard word and a liberating one. It removes the freedom to select an audience and to edit a message, and it removes the burden of having to invent something worth saying.

Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, declares the LORD."

God names the real problem. It is not inability; it is fear. Jeremiah will be beaten, put in the stocks, thrown into a cistern and accused of treason, so the fear is not irrational. The remedy given is not a promise that they will listen, or that he will be liked. It is a presence: I am with you.

That is the same word the risen Christ left with his church when he sent it into the world: And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20). And it is what Paul heard in Corinth when he was afraid: Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you (Acts 18:9-10). Is there a conversation you are avoiding because of what the person might say back?

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD put out his hand and touched my mouth. And the LORD said to me, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. See, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the LORD put out his hand and touched my mouth. And the LORD said to me, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.

The objection was about a mouth, so God touches his mouth. Isaiah's lips were touched with a coal from the altar to deal with his guilt: Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for (Isa 6:7). Here the touch is a commission: the words themselves are put in.

Ezekiel was made to eat a scroll (Ezek 3:1-3), and John in Revelation ate a little scroll that was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter (Rev 10:10). That is Jeremiah's life in a sentence. The word of God is sweet to receive and bitter to carry.

See, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant."

A village boy is set over nations and over kingdoms. Not with an army; with a message. The empires of his day would have laughed. They are gone, and his words are still being read.

Six verbs, and count them: four tear down, two build. That is the proportion of this book, and it is honest about what the word of God must do in a place that has gone wrong. You cannot plant in ground that has not been cleared. Paul describes his ministry the same way: weapons with divine power to destroy strongholds, demolishing arguments so that thoughts can be taken captive to Christ (2 Cor 10:4-5).

But the two constructive verbs are not an afterthought, and later in this book God takes them up again: as I have watched over them to pluck up and break down, so I will watch over them to build and to plant (31:28). The book that begins with demolition ends with a new covenant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Two Visions: the Almond and the Boiling Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I see an almond branch, and the LORD answers, I am watching over my word to perform it (vv. 11-12). Then I see a boiling pot, facing away from the north, and out of the north disaster is let loose (vv. 13-14). The kingdoms of the north will set their thrones at the gates of Jerusalem (v. 15), and God will declare his judgments for all their evil in forsaking me (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God watches over his word to do it, and the first thing it will do here is bring an army from the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Jeremiah, what do you see?" And I said, "I see an almond branch." Then the LORD said to me, "You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Jeremiah, what do you see?" And I said, "I see an almond branch."

The first vision is almost domestic: a branch in blossom, the sort of thing anyone might notice on a walk. God asks him what he sees, because God is about to teach him to read ordinary things.

Then the LORD said to me, "You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it."

The answer turns on a play on words that English cannot carry, and the ESV's footnote preserves it: "Almond sounds like the Hebrew for watching". Jeremiah sees an almond branch, and God says, I am the watching God, and what I am watching over is my word.

That is the sentence to hold for the next fifty-one chapters. Everything God says in this book will happen. Not one syllable of it will fall to the ground unattended. So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose (Isa 55:11). Has he said, and will he not do it? (Num 23:19).

It cuts both ways, which is exactly why it is here. For a prophet who will preach for forty years and see almost no response, it means his labour is not wasted. For a nation that has heard the warnings and shrugged, it means the warnings are not noise. God is awake over what he has said.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me a second time, saying, "What do you see?" And I said, "I see a boiling pot, facing away from the north." Then the LORD said to me, "Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land. For behold, I am calling all the tribes of the kingdoms of the north, declares the LORD, and they shall come, and every one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, against all its walls all around and against all the cities of Judah. And I will declare my judgments against them, for all their evil in forsaking me. They have made offerings to other gods and worshiped the works of their own hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me a second time, saying, "What do you see?" And I said, "I see a boiling pot, facing away from the north."

The second vision is a cooking pot at the boil, tilted so that what is inside is about to pour out, and the tilt is away from the north. Something is about to spill over Judah, and it is coming from up there.

Then the LORD said to me, "Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land.

The ESV notes that the word rendered disaster can mean evil, harm or disaster depending on the context, and that this is so throughout Jeremiah. The armies came from the north because the desert lay to the east; that is the road every invader took. Within Jeremiah's lifetime Babylon would come down it.

For behold, I am calling all the tribes of the kingdoms of the north, declares the LORD, and they shall come, and every one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, against all its walls all around and against all the cities of Judah.

Notice who is doing it: I am calling. Babylon thought it was pursuing its own ambitions. It was being summoned. The thrones set in the gateway are the picture of a conquered city, with foreign officials sitting where Judah's elders used to give judgment.

And I will declare my judgments against them, for all their evil in forsaking me. They have made offerings to other gods and worshiped the works of their own hands."

And the reason is given plainly, so that no one can call the disaster meaningless. It is not bad luck or geopolitics. It is forsaking me, and the shape that forsaking took: worshipping the works of their own hands. They made something, then bowed to it. Every generation does, and the objects change.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–19 — An Iron Pillar and Bronze Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But you, dress yourself for work; arise, and say to them everything that I command you, and do not be dismayed (v. 17). God makes him a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against the whole land, its kings, officials and priests (v. 18). They will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not promise the prophet an easy audience; he promises to make him able to stand and to keep him through it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, dress yourself for work; arise, and say to them everything that I command you. Do not be dismayed by them, lest I dismay you before them. And I, behold, I make you this day a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls, against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, dress yourself for work; arise, and say to them everything that I command you. Do not be dismayed by them, lest I dismay you before them.

The ESV notes that dress yourself for work is in Hebrew "gird up your loins": gather the long robe, tie it at the waist, get ready to move. It is the posture of a man about to run or to fight.

Then a warning with a sting in it: Do not be dismayed by them, lest I dismay you before them. Fear of the audience is not a small weakness to be indulged in a preacher; it is the thing that will break him in public. If he will not fear God more than the crowd, God will let the crowd frighten him. The cure for the fear of people is not courage summoned from inside. It is the fear of God, which crowds out every lesser fear.

And I, behold, I make you this day a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls, against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land.

Three images, all of them defensive and immovable: a walled city, an iron pillar, walls of bronze. God does not remove the opposition, and he lists exactly who it will be: the palace, the civil service, the clergy and the public. Everyone. Instead of removing them, he makes the man able to stand.

Ezekiel received the same kind of hardening: Behold, I have made your face as hard as their faces, Fear them not, nor be dismayed at their looks (Ezek 3:8-9). God gives what the calling requires, and he gives it to the person who has just said he cannot do it.

verseByVerse.quote: They will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you, declares the LORD, to deliver you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you, declares the LORD, to deliver you."

The chapter ends with the promise it began building toward, and it is worded with great care. Not, they will not fight you. They will fight against you — that is stated as fact. But they shall not prevail.

Read Jeremiah's life before deciding what that promise covers. He was put in stocks, thrown into a muddy cistern and left to sink, imprisoned, accused of desertion, ignored by kings who burned his scroll, and finally carried off to Egypt by people who refused his advice. He was not protected from any of it. He was preserved through all of it, and the word he carried outlived every one of his opponents.

Jesus said of his church, on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt 16:18), and told his disciples, In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33). If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom 8:31).

And there is one prophet of whom this promise was not made in that form. Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem and was preserved; Christ wept over the same city (Luke 19:41) and was handed over to it. He had the words of God in his mouth in a way no prophet ever had, speaking only what to say and what to speak from his Father (John 12:49), and when they fought against him, he did not call for deliverance. He was the prophet Moses promised, The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers (Acts 3:22), and he was not delivered, so that we would be.

1.title: The Call of Jeremiah: I Am Watching Over My Word
1.overview:
Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, received the word of the LORD from the thirteenth year of Josiah until Jerusalem went into captivity: about forty years of preaching that ended with his country in ruins (vv. 1-3).

God tells him that he knew, consecrated and appointed him before he was born (vv. 4-5). Jeremiah objects that he cannot speak and is only a youth; God forbids the excuse, sends him where he will be sent to say what he will be given, and promises, I am with you to deliver you (vv. 6-8). God touches his mouth, puts his words in it, and sets him over nations to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (vv. 9-10).

Two visions follow. An almond branch: I am watching over my word to perform it (vv. 11-12). A boiling pot tilted from the north: an invasion God himself is summoning, because his people have forsaken him for the works of their own hands (vv. 13-16). Finally Jeremiah is told to get ready and not to be dismayed, and God makes him a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls: they will fight him and will not prevail (vv. 17-19).
1.theology:
God's call rests on his own prior choice, not on the one called (vv. 4-5; Ps 139:16; Gal 1:15), and he deals with the unborn as persons he knows and appoints. Fitness for service is not self-confidence but God's presence and God's words (vv. 6-9; Exod 4:11-12; Matt 28:20).

The word of God does demolishing work before it builds (v. 10; 2 Cor 10:4-5), and the building is promised (31:28). God watches over his word to perform it, so that neither warning nor promise falls to the ground (v. 12; Isa 55:11; Num 23:19).

God governs the nations that punish his people: the invader from the north is summoned by him (v. 15). Fear of man is the prophet's real danger, and the remedy is the fear of God (v. 17). God does not remove opposition but makes his servant able to stand and preserves him through it (vv. 18-19; Matt 16:18) — as he did not preserve his Son, the prophet greater than Jeremiah (Acts 3:22; Luke 19:41).
1.examples:
Forty years of faithful preaching that ended in national ruin.

Judging a ministry by results rather than by faithfulness.

God's answer to "I can't": not "you are better than you think", but "I am with you".

A scroll sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach.

Four verbs that tear down and two that build.

The conversation you are avoiding because of what they might say back.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to me, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem, Thus says the LORD, "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.<sup>3</sup>Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest. All who ate of it incurred guilt; disaster came upon them, declares the LORD."<sup>4</sup>Hear the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Thus says the LORD: "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless?<sup>6</sup>They did not say, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us in the wilderness, in a land of deserts and pits, in a land of drought and deep darkness, in a land that none passes through, where no man dwells?'<sup>7</sup>And I brought you into a plentiful land to enjoy its fruits and its good things. But when you came in, you defiled my land and made my heritage an abomination.<sup>8</sup>The priests did not say, 'Where is the LORD?' Those who handle the law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal and went after things that do not profit.<sup>9</sup>"Therefore I still contend with you, declares the LORD, and with your children's children I will contend.<sup>10</sup>For cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see, or send to Kedar and examine with care; see if there has been such a thing.<sup>11</sup>Has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit.<sup>12</sup>Be appalled, O heavens, at this; be shocked, be utterly desolate, declares the LORD,<sup>13</sup>for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.<sup>14</sup>"Is Israel a slave? Is he a homeborn servant? Why then has he become a prey?<sup>15</sup>The lions have roared against him; they have roared loudly. They have made his land a waste; his cities are in ruins, without inhabitant.<sup>16</sup>Moreover, the men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved the crown of your head.<sup>17</sup>Have you not brought this upon yourself by forsaking the LORD your God, when he led you in the way?<sup>18</sup>And now what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates?<sup>19</sup>Your evil will chastise you, and your apostasy will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to forsake the LORD your God; the fear of me is not in you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.<sup>20</sup>"For long ago I broke your yoke and burst your bonds; but you said, 'I will not serve.' Yes, on every high hill and under every green tree you bowed down like a whore.<sup>21</sup>Yet I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed. How then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine?<sup>22</sup>Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>23</sup>How can you say, 'I am not unclean, I have not gone after the Baals'? Look at your way in the valley; know what you have done— a restless young camel running here and there,<sup>24</sup>a wild donkey used to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust? None who seek her need weary themselves; in her month they will find her.<sup>25</sup>Keep your feet from going unshod and your throat from thirst. But you said, 'It is hopeless, for I have loved foreigners, and after them I will go.'<sup>26</sup>"As a thief is shamed when caught, so the house of Israel shall be shamed: they, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets,<sup>27</sup>who say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth.' For they have turned their back to me, and not their face. But in the time of their trouble they say, 'Arise and save us!'<sup>28</sup>But where are your gods that you made for yourself? Let them arise, if they can save you, in your time of trouble; for as many as your cities are your gods, O Judah.<sup>29</sup>"Why do you contend with me? You have all transgressed against me, declares the LORD.<sup>30</sup>In vain have I struck your children; they took no correction; your own sword devoured your prophets like a ravening lion.<sup>31</sup>And you, O generation, behold the word of the LORD. Have I been a wilderness to Israel, or a land of thick darkness? Why then do my people say, 'We are free, we will come no more to you'?<sup>32</sup>Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me days without number.<sup>33</sup>"How well you direct your course to seek love! So that even to wicked women you have taught your ways.<sup>34</sup>Also on your skirts is found the lifeblood of the guiltless poor; you did not find them breaking in. Yet in spite of all these things<sup>35</sup>you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned.'<sup>36</sup>How much you go about, changing your way! You shall be put to shame by Egypt as you were put to shame by Assyria.<sup>37</sup>From it too you will come away with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust, and you will not prosper by them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Devotion of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends Jeremiah to Jerusalem with a memory: I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness (vv. 1-3). Then the question: What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless? (vv. 4-5). They never asked Where is the LORD who brought them up from Egypt (v. 6); brought into a plentiful land, they defiled it (v. 7), and priests, lawyers, shepherds and prophets all failed together (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God begins not with accusation but with memory: he recalls the love of the early days, and asks what he did to deserve being left.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem, Thus says the LORD, "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown. Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest. All who ate of it incurred guilt; disaster came upon them, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem, Thus says the LORD, "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.

The first sermon of the book does not open with an accusation. It opens with a memory, and it is God's memory. I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride.

He is thinking of the exodus and the wilderness years, and he describes them the way a husband describes the early days of a marriage. There was a time when they followed him anywhere, into a land not sown, with no crops and no guarantees, simply because he was going that way.

That is a remarkable thing for God to say about the wilderness generation, because the books of Exodus and Numbers are full of their grumbling. He remembers the love, and does not rehearse the complaints. Grace has a long memory for the good.

Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest. All who ate of it incurred guilt; disaster came upon them, declares the LORD."

Firstfruits were the portion given to God and reserved for him alone; anyone else who ate them was guilty. That is what Israel was to him: set apart, his own, protected by his jealousy so that whoever touched them answered for it.

Before you read a word of the indictment, notice the tone. This is not a landlord evicting a tenant. It is a husband remembering a honeymoon, and it is about to become one of the saddest chapters in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel. Thus says the LORD: "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless? They did not say, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us in the wilderness, in a land of deserts and pits, in a land of drought and deep darkness, in a land that none passes through, where no man dwells?' And I brought you into a plentiful land to enjoy its fruits and its good things. But when you came in, you defiled my land and made my heritage an abomination. The priests did not say, 'Where is the LORD?' Those who handle the law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal and went after things that do not profit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless?

Here is the question at the heart of the chapter, and God is the one asking it. What wrong did your fathers find in me? Not, what did you gain by leaving; what fault did you find? He invites them to produce the complaint, the grievance, the thing he did that justified it. There is none.

And then a line worth stopping over: went after worthlessness, and became worthless. The word is the same on both sides. You become what you worship. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps 115:8). Paul says the same of the human race: they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images, and their foolish hearts were darkened (Rom 1:21-23). Worship is never neutral; it is formative. Whatever you give yourself to is shaping you into its own likeness right now.

They did not say, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us in the wilderness, in a land of deserts and pits, in a land of drought and deep darkness, in a land that none passes through, where no man dwells?'

The failure was not a decision to reject God. It was a question they stopped asking. Nobody said, where is the LORD? The rescue was still in the history books and had gone out of the conversation. That is how faith is usually lost: not in a crisis of belief, but in a slow silence.

And I brought you into a plentiful land to enjoy its fruits and its good things. But when you came in, you defiled my land and made my heritage an abomination.

God gave them a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity (Deut 8:9), and the gift became the occasion of the forgetting. Prosperity is harder on faith than poverty, because it removes the daily sense of need.

The priests did not say, 'Where is the LORD?' Those who handle the law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal and went after things that do not profit.

Then the leadership, four groups, and every one has failed. The priests, who ran the worship, never asked where God was. The scholars who handle the law did not know its author. The shepherds — the ESV notes that the word may be rendered "rulers" — broke the covenant themselves. And the preachers preached another god entirely. When a nation collapses spiritually, it is rarely the people who fall first.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No nation changes its gods, But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit (vv. 9-11). Heaven is called to be appalled, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water (vv. 12-13). The lions have roared and the land is waste (vv. 14-16). Have you not brought this upon yourself by forsaking the LORD your God, running to Egypt and Assyria for water (vv. 17-19)?
verseByVerse.theology: Sin here is two acts, not one: leaving the spring, and digging a tank that cannot hold water.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I still contend with you, declares the LORD, and with your children's children I will contend. For cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see, or send to Kedar and examine with care; see if there has been such a thing. Has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit. Be appalled, O heavens, at this; be shocked, be utterly desolate, declares the LORD, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore I still contend with you, declares the LORD, and with your children's children I will contend. For cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see, or send to Kedar and examine with care; see if there has been such a thing.

God takes them to court, and the case rests on a survey. Send west to Cyprus, send east to Kedar, and ask a simple question: does anyone do this?

Has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit.

The pagans, God says, are more loyal to gods that do not exist than my people are to me. No nation trades in its deities. Israel traded their glory — the living God himself, their honour and their boast — for something that does not profit. It is not only wicked; it is a spectacularly bad deal.

Be appalled, O heavens, at this; be shocked, be utterly desolate, declares the LORD,

Heaven is called as witness, and told to be horrified. Sin has become so normal on earth that the reaction has to be imported from somewhere else.

for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.

Here is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward, and it is one of the clearest definitions of sin in Scripture. Not one evil, but two.

The first is leaving. God is the fountain of living waters: a spring, moving, fresh, free, endlessly replenished, requiring no work from anyone but a cupped hand. In a hot country that is not poetry; it is life.

The second is the substitute. A cistern is a pit cut out of rock to hold rainwater. Cutting one is brutal labour, months of it. The water it holds is still, warm and stale at best. And these are broken cisterns: cracked, so that the water drains away and the digger is left with a dry hole he spent his strength on.

That is the anatomy of every sin: a real spring abandoned, and enormous effort spent on a leaking substitute. Nobody works harder than someone trying to get from a career, a relationship, a bottle or an image what only God gives. And the cistern always leaks, which is why it must be dug again next year.

Jesus stood in the temple and answered this verse directly: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). To a woman drawing water he said, whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again (John 4:14). And at the end of the Bible the offer still stands: To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment (Rev 21:6). Without payment. The fountain is free; only the cisterns cost.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is Israel a slave? Is he a homeborn servant? Why then has he become a prey? The lions have roared against him; they have roared loudly. They have made his land a waste; his cities are in ruins, without inhabitant. Moreover, the men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved the crown of your head. Have you not brought this upon yourself by forsaking the LORD your God, when he led you in the way? And now what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates? Your evil will chastise you, and your apostasy will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to forsake the LORD your God; the fear of me is not in you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Is Israel a slave? Is he a homeborn servant? Why then has he become a prey? The lions have roared against him; they have roared loudly. They have made his land a waste; his cities are in ruins, without inhabitant.

Three questions and a scene of ruin. Israel was God's son, not anyone's slave, so why is he being carried off like plunder? The lions are the empires, and the roaring has already begun: towns burned, fields wasted, villages emptied.

Moreover, the men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved the crown of your head.

Memphis and Tahpanhes are Egyptian cities, and the shaved crown is the mark of a slave or a mourner. The ESV notes that have shaved is in Hebrew "grazed". The allies Judah courted have treated her like pasture.

Have you not brought this upon yourself by forsaking the LORD your God, when he led you in the way?

The question refuses every comfortable explanation. Not the empires, not bad luck, not God's neglect. Have you not brought this upon yourself? There is a kind of pain that is simply the shape of our own choices coming back to us.

And now what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates?

The water image returns, now as foreign policy. Judah's politics swung between the two superpowers, drinking first from the Nile and then from the Euphrates, buying protection with tribute and treaties. The ESV notes that the Nile is in Hebrew "Shihor" and the Euphrates "the River". Every generation has its version of this: the fear that God is not enough, and the search for a stronger friend.

Your evil will chastise you, and your apostasy will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to forsake the LORD your God; the fear of me is not in you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.

God does not need to invent a punishment; the sin administers its own. Your evil will chastise you. The psalm says it as a judicial act: So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels (Ps 81:12). Sometimes the severest thing God does is let a person have what he insisted on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — The Choice Vine Gone Wild
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will not serve, said the people, bowing on every high hill (v. 20). Planted a choice vine, wholly of pure seed, they turned degenerate (v. 21), and no amount of lye and soap removes the stain (v. 22). They deny it (v. 23), though they run like a wild donkey in heat (vv. 24-25). Israel will be shamed like a caught thief (v. 26), saying to a tree You are my father, and in trouble crying Arise and save us! (v. 27). But where are your gods that you made for yourself? (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry is both a slavery that cannot be broken by willpower and a stain that cannot be scrubbed out.

verseByVerse.quote: "For long ago I broke your yoke and burst your bonds; but you said, 'I will not serve.' Yes, on every high hill and under every green tree you bowed down like a whore. Yet I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed. How then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine? Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For long ago I broke your yoke and burst your bonds; but you said, 'I will not serve.' Yes, on every high hill and under every green tree you bowed down like a whore.

God broke the yoke in Egypt, and the freed slave answered, I will not serve — not him, at least. And then he bowed anyway, on every hill and under every tree, to whatever local shrine was going. Nobody serves nothing. The yoke thrown off is always replaced.

Yet I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed. How then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine?

The gardener chose the best stock and planted it himself, and what came up was wild. The fault cannot be traced to the seed or the gardener. It is in what the vine has done with the soil it was given.

Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me, declares the Lord GOD.

Now the image changes to laundry, and it settles the question of self-improvement. Lye and soap were the strongest cleaners available. Scrub as hard as you like: the stain of your guilt is still before me. Before him — that is the problem. It is not about feeling clean.

This verse leaves only one door open, and the New Testament opens it: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). The stain that no effort removes is removed by confession and by blood, and by nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: How can you say, 'I am not unclean, I have not gone after the Baals'? Look at your way in the valley; know what you have done— a restless young camel running here and there, a wild donkey used to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust? None who seek her need weary themselves; in her month they will find her. Keep your feet from going unshod and your throat from thirst. But you said, 'It is hopeless, for I have loved foreigners, and after them I will go.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can you say, 'I am not unclean, I have not gone after the Baals'? Look at your way in the valley; know what you have done— a restless young camel running here and there,

The denial is quoted back at them, and answered with evidence: Look at your way in the valley. The valley of Hinnom below Jerusalem is where children were burned to Molech. Do not tell me what you believe; look at what you have done.

a wild donkey used to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust? None who seek her need weary themselves; in her month they will find her.

The images are deliberately undignified: a young camel bolting in every direction, a wild donkey in heat that nobody needs to chase because she comes to them. This is what idolatry does to a people. It is not sophisticated. It is compulsive.

And it is honest about addiction: Who can restrain her lust? The question expects the answer nobody, and certainly not the animal herself. Anyone who has tried to break a habit by willpower alone knows the verse from the inside.

Keep your feet from going unshod and your throat from thirst. But you said, 'It is hopeless, for I have loved foreigners, and after them I will go.'

God pleads with them to stop wearing out their shoes and their throats chasing what will not feed them. The reply is the saddest line in the chapter: It is hopeless. Not defiance, but despair. I am too far gone; this is who I am now. Many people are held in something they hate by exactly that sentence, and it is a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: "As a thief is shamed when caught, so the house of Israel shall be shamed: they, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets, who say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth.' For they have turned their back to me, and not their face. But in the time of their trouble they say, 'Arise and save us!' But where are your gods that you made for yourself? Let them arise, if they can save you, in your time of trouble; for as many as your cities are your gods, O Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As a thief is shamed when caught, so the house of Israel shall be shamed: they, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets,

The shame of a thief is not remorse for stealing; it is the shame of being caught. That is the shame coming to Judah, and the list runs from the palace down: kings, officials, priests, prophets. The same four groups as verse 8. The failure is systemic and named.

who say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth.' For they have turned their back to me, and not their face. But in the time of their trouble they say, 'Arise and save us!'

Two sentences that between them describe most religion. In good times, a tree is my father and a stone gave me birth: whatever I have made is what I am from. In bad times, Arise and save us!, addressed to the God whose back they have been looking at.

God notices the posture: they have turned their back to me, and not their face. That is the difference between a wandering child and a settled rebellion, and it is also the whole of repentance. Turning round is all that is required, and it is the one thing they will not do.

But where are your gods that you made for yourself? Let them arise, if they can save you, in your time of trouble; for as many as your cities are your gods, O Judah.

The irony is sharp: your gods that you made for yourself. Call them, God says. See if they stand up. Isaiah put it the same way: Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing? (Isa 44:10). And there were plenty of them — a god for every town, and not one of them able to move.

The test still works. When the diagnosis comes, or the job goes, or the marriage cracks, you find out very quickly which of the things you serve can stand up and help.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's discipline taught them nothing, and their own sword killed the prophets (vv. 29-30). Have I been a wilderness to Israel?, he asks, when they say We are free, we will come no more to you (v. 31). Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me days without number (v. 32). With the blood of the guiltless poor on their skirts they still say I am innocent (vv. 33-35), and Egypt will shame them as Assyria did (vv. 36-37).
verseByVerse.theology: The final defence of a guilty people is not argument but denial, and God answers it by bringing them to judgment for the denial itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you contend with me? You have all transgressed against me, declares the LORD. In vain have I struck your children; they took no correction; your own sword devoured your prophets like a ravening lion. And you, O generation, behold the word of the LORD. Have I been a wilderness to Israel, or a land of thick darkness? Why then do my people say, 'We are free, we will come no more to you'? Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me days without number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Why do you contend with me? You have all transgressed against me, declares the LORD. In vain have I struck your children; they took no correction; your own sword devoured your prophets like a ravening lion.

They are arguing with him, and he asks why. Then two sentences of terrible summary: the discipline achieved nothing — they took no correction — and the messengers sent to explain the discipline were killed. A nation that will neither feel a warning nor hear an explanation has closed both doors.

And you, O generation, behold the word of the LORD. Have I been a wilderness to Israel, or a land of thick darkness? Why then do my people say, 'We are free, we will come no more to you'?

The question of verse 5 returns, sharper. Have I been a wilderness to Israel? Have I been barren ground to you? Have I been the dark place you had to escape? God asks to be shown the evidence for the way he is being treated.

And the answer his people give is the oldest lie about God there is: We are free, we will come no more to you. Freedom is defined as distance from him. It is exactly what the serpent suggested, and what every generation repeats. In three chapters' time the same people will be described as slaves of what they chose.

Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me days without number.

A bride does not forget her dress. It is not possible; it is the most precious thing she owns and the day is the biggest of her life. Yet my people have forgotten me days without number.

Read that slowly, because it is not an accusation of atheism. It is an accusation of forgetting, and forgetting does not feel like rebellion. It feels like being busy. God measures it in days: how many days without number have gone by, with no thought of him at all?

verseByVerse.quote: "How well you direct your course to seek love! So that even to wicked women you have taught your ways. Also on your skirts is found the lifeblood of the guiltless poor; you did not find them breaking in. Yet in spite of all these things you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned.' How much you go about, changing your way! You shall be put to shame by Egypt as you were put to shame by Assyria. From it too you will come away with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust, and you will not prosper by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How well you direct your course to seek love! So that even to wicked women you have taught your ways. Also on your skirts is found the lifeblood of the guiltless poor; you did not find them breaking in. Yet in spite of all these things

Two charges together, and their pairing is the point. They have become expert at pursuing love in all the wrong places, so accomplished that the professionals could learn from them. And there is blood on their clothes: the lifeblood of the guiltless poor, people who were not caught breaking in, who had done nothing.

Idolatry and injustice arrive together, always. A people who will worship anything will eventually spend anyone. The prophets never separate the two, and neither should we.

you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned.'

With blood on the hem, the claim is I am innocent. And notice what God says he will judge. Not only the sin, but the denial of it: I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned.'

That is a sobering line, and also a hopeful one. It means the one thing standing between this people and mercy is the sentence they keep repeating. The next chapter will show God pleading for one word of acknowledgement (3:13), and it is the same word the New Testament asks for. Self-defence is the only posture in which forgiveness cannot be received.

How much you go about, changing your way! You shall be put to shame by Egypt as you were put to shame by Assyria. From it too you will come away with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust, and you will not prosper by them."

The chapter ends with restless diplomacy: first Assyria, now Egypt, always changing, always looking for a better arrangement. They will come home from Egypt with your hands on your head, the posture of prisoners and mourners.

The reason is given last and it is final: the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust. Every refuge that is not God is a refuge God has already rejected. Better to learn that before the crisis than during it.

2.title: Two Evils: The Fountain and the Broken Cisterns
2.overview:
God sends Jeremiah to Jerusalem with a memory of the early days: I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride (vv. 1-3). Then he asks what wrong they found in him, that they went after worthlessness and became worthless; they stopped asking where he was, defiled the land he gave them, and their priests, scholars, rulers and prophets all failed (vv. 4-8).

No nation changes its gods, yet Israel exchanged its glory for what does not profit (vv. 9-11). Heaven is called to be appalled at two evils: forsaking the fountain of living waters, and digging broken cisterns that hold no water (vv. 12-13). The ruin that has come is self-inflicted, and running to Egypt and Assyria for help will not mend it (vv. 14-19).

The freed slave said I will not serve and bowed to idols anyway; the choice vine turned wild; no soap removes the stain (vv. 20-22). Denial is answered with evidence, and the people say their case is hopeless (vv. 23-25). They call a tree their father and cry to God only in trouble (vv. 26-28). Discipline taught them nothing, and a bride who could never forget her dress has forgotten God without number (vv. 29-32). With the blood of the poor on their clothes they plead innocence, and God will judge them for the plea (vv. 33-37).
2.theology:
Sin is defined here in two movements: forsaking God, the fountain of living waters, and constructing substitutes that cannot hold what they promise (v. 13). Christ answers the first half by offering living water freely (John 4:14; 7:37; Rev 21:6).

Worship is formative: those who go after worthlessness become worthless (v. 5; Ps 115:8; Rom 1:21-23). Prosperity and forgetfulness, not argument, are how faith is usually lost (vv. 6-7, 32). Leaders fail first (vv. 8, 26).

Sin carries its own punishment (v. 19; Ps 81:12), cannot be washed out by self-improvement (v. 22; 1 John 1:9), and is most dangerous when denied: God judges the claim I have not sinned (v. 35). Idolatry and injustice always travel together (vv. 33-34).
2.examples:
A husband remembering a honeymoon before naming a betrayal.

Faith lost not in a crisis of belief but in a slow silence.

Months of labour cutting a tank that leaks, beside a free spring.

Lye and soap on a stain that is before God, not before you.

"It is hopeless" — despair, not defiance, keeping people where they are.

A bride who could not forget her dress.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>"If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD.<sup>2</sup>Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom.<sup>3</sup>Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed.<sup>4</sup>Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth—<sup>5</sup>will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."<sup>6</sup>The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore?<sup>7</sup>And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it.<sup>8</sup>She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore.<sup>9</sup>Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree.<sup>10</sup>Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.<sup>12</sup>Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever.<sup>13</sup>Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.<sup>14</sup>Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion.<sup>15</sup>"'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.<sup>16</sup>And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again.<sup>17</sup>At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart.<sup>18</sup>In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.<sup>19</sup>"'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me.<sup>20</sup>Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"<sup>21</sup>A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God.<sup>22</sup>"Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness." "Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God.<sup>23</sup>Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.<sup>24</sup>"But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters.<sup>25</sup>Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Would You Return to Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law says a divorced wife who has married another cannot go back to her first husband; You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? (v. 1). The bare heights show where she has been, and the rains have been withheld, yet you refuse to be ashamed (vv. 2-3). She still calls him My father, you are the friend of my youth and asks whether he will be angry forever, Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Affectionate words to God alongside unchanged behaviour are not repentance; and yet the impossible invitation to return is the one God makes.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD. Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed. Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth— will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD.

The chapter opens with a point of law. Under Deuteronomy, a man who divorced his wife could not take her back once she had married someone else: her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD (Deut 24:4). The case is closed. The door is shut by God's own statute.

And then, in the same breath, God says: would you return to me?

That is the astonishing thing in this chapter, and everything else stands under it. What the law forbids, love offers. God is not pretending the marriage was undamaged or the adultery small — many lovers is his own phrase — and he still opens a door the law had bolted. How he can do this without ceasing to be just is the question the whole Bible answers at the cross.

Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom.

The invitation does not come with amnesia. Look up at the hilltops, God says: every one of them has a shrine, and you have been at all of them. The picture of sitting by the roadside waiting is worse than being seduced. It is initiative.

Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed.

The drought was a message, and it was missed. The forehead of a whore is a face that has lost the capacity to blush. Shame is painful and it is a mercy; a conscience that can still be embarrassed is still alive. The danger point in any life is not doing wrong but reaching the stage of doing it without a flicker.

Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth— will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."

And here is the most uncomfortable verse in the chapter, because the words are lovely. My father, you are the friend of my youth. Warm, intimate, theologically correct, and quite compatible with having done all the evil that you could. Religious language is not repentance. It is possible to call God Father in one breath and keep every arrangement he hates in the next, and this verse exists to stop us doing it comfortably.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Faithless Israel and Treacherous Judah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Josiah's days God shows Jeremiah faithless Israel, who would not return, and her sister Judah who watched (vv. 6-7). Israel was sent away with a decree of divorce, and Judah still did not fear but played the whore too (vv. 8-9), returning not with her whole heart, but in pretense (v. 10). So Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah (v. 11), and northward goes the call: Return, faithless Israel, Only acknowledge your guilt (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Watching judgment fall on someone else and learning nothing is worse than the sin that brought it; and the way back is one honest admission.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore? And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it. She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore. Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree. Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore?

Now a history lesson with two sisters in it. Israel is the northern kingdom, which had already been destroyed by Assyria a century before Jeremiah preached. Judah is the southern kingdom, still standing, listening to this sermon.

And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it.

Two things to notice. First, God says, After she has done all this she will return to me — the language of a patient husband waiting at the window, which is how God describes his own long-suffering. Second, her treacherous sister Judah saw it. Judah had a front-row seat at her sister's funeral.

She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore.

Judah watched the exile of the north — the deportations, the ruined towns, the end of a nation — and drew no conclusion at all. Judah did not fear. There is no education in watching judgment fall on someone else if you have decided in advance that it cannot happen to you.

Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree. Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."

She took her whoredom lightly — that is how nations and people fall, not by deciding sin is good but by deciding it is small. And Judah's response is named exactly: she did return, but in pretense.

This is said in the days of King Josiah, during the great national reform: the idols were smashed, the temple repaired, the Passover kept. It was genuine at the top, and it never reached the heart of the people. A reformation of behaviour without a change of heart is what God calls pretence, and he can tell the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah. Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.

A shocking verdict. The northern kingdom, whose name was a byword for apostasy, comes out better than Judah. Israel sinned with no warning example in front of her; Judah sinned having watched the consequences, while holding the temple, the law, the priesthood and the promises. Privilege raises the bar. The more light, the greater the guilt.

Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever.

And then Jeremiah is told to face north — toward the people who are already gone, scattered a hundred years ago into Assyria, a lost cause by every reckoning — and preach to them. Return, faithless Israel.

The reasons given are all about God: I am merciful, I will not be angry forever. Not, you are not as bad as you think. The ground of the invitation is his character, which is the only ground any of us has.

Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.

And here is the whole requirement, in one word: Only acknowledge your guilt.

Only. Not make restitution first, not clean yourself up, not produce a period of good behaviour to prove you mean it. Say what is true. Chapter 2 ended with a people insisting I have not sinned (2:35); this is the exact reverse, and it is the door. Joel says it the same way: return to me with all your heart, rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:12-13). Hosea gives the words to use: Take with you words and return to the LORD (Hos 14:2). And John says it to the church: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Shepherds After My Own Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Return, O faithless children, for God is their master, and he will bring them to Zion one from a city and two from a family (v. 14), giving them shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding (v. 15). The ark will not be remembered or missed (v. 16); Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it (v. 17), and Judah and Israel will come home together (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is small in its beginnings, pastoral in its care, and larger than Israel at its end.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion. "'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding. And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again. At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart. In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion.

The call is repeated, and the promise attached to it is deliberately modest: one from a city and two from a family. God is not predicting a national landslide. He is describing a remnant, gathered person by person out of places that will not come as a whole.

That is usually how it works. Revival is talked about in national terms; it arrives one person and two people at a time, and God calls that homecoming.

"'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.

Chapter 2 exposed shepherds who transgressed against me (2:8). Here is the remedy: not better management but men whose hearts match God's, and whose work is feeding. The phrase echoes what God said of David, a man after my heart, who will do all my will (Acts 13:22). The risen Christ still gives the shepherds and teachers to his church (Eph 4:11), and behind every faithful one stands the good shepherd himself.

And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again.

The most sacred object in Israel's worship — the ark, the throne of God's presence, the centre of the holy of holies — will not be missed. Not destroyed and mourned; simply not needed, and not thought of.

That is not a downgrade but a promotion. A sign becomes unnecessary when the thing it signified has arrived in person. The next verse says what replaces it.

At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart. In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.

Three enormous promises. The whole city becomes the throne room, not one gold box inside one room. All nations gather, not Israel alone. And the heart itself changes: they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart — which is exactly what chapter 31 will call the new covenant. The divided kingdoms come home together, the family reunited.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me (v. 19), but Israel was treacherous as a wife who leaves (v. 20). Weeping is heard on the bare heights (v. 21), and God says, Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness (v. 22). The people answer that the hills were a delusion and salvation is in the LORD (vv. 23-24), and lie down in their shame: we have sinned against the LORD our God (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: God heals faithlessness rather than merely forgiving it, and the confession that follows is the evidence, not the condition.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me. Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me.

This is God speaking about his own hopes, and it is almost unbearable to read. How I would set you among my sons. He wanted to treat them as children, to give them the best land there was, to hear them call him Father.

Scripture is not embarrassed to show God like this. How can I give you up, O Ephraim?, he says through Hosea; My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (Hos 11:8). Whatever else the judgment in this book is, it is not the cold act of a God who never wanted anything else.

Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"

And the sentence lands with the marriage image again. Not a tenant breaking a lease. A wife walking out. The offence is measured by the intimacy it violated, which is why sin against God is never merely rule-breaking.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God. "Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness." "Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God. Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel. "But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God.

The bare heights were the scene of the idolatry in verse 2. Now the same hills carry a different sound: weeping. The place of the sin becomes the place of the sorrow over it.

"Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness."

Eight words that contain the gospel of this chapter. Notice what God promises to do. Not merely to forgive the faithlessness, but to heal it. He treats the disloyalty as a disease in his people rather than only a debt against himself, and he undertakes the cure.

That is the only reason anyone returns at all. If the invitation were simply "come back and do better", it would sink the very people it calls, who have already proved they cannot. The offer is that the God who is wronged will himself repair the capacity to love him.

"Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God. Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.

And they answer. Behold, we come to you. The ESV notes that a delusion is in Hebrew "commotion": all that noise on the hilltops, all that energy, and nothing in it. Repentance always includes a revised opinion of what we left God for. They now see the shrines as they are.

But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."

The confession is complete and it is costly. They add up what idolatry took: the livestock, the harvests, the children given to Molech — all for which our fathers labored. Sin is finally accounted for not as pleasure but as loss.

And they do not minimise: we have sinned, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day. No blaming the ancestors alone, no limiting it to a bad season. Compare chapter 2, where the same people said I am innocent (2:35). This is what the turn looks like, and it comes after the promise to heal, not before it. The kindness is what makes the confession possible.

3.title: Return, Faithless Israel: I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
3.overview:
The law says a wife who has left her husband for another cannot return, yet God asks his adulterous people, would you return to me? (v. 1). The hills show where they have been, the rains have been withheld, and they have lost the ability to blush (vv. 2-3). They still use affectionate words about God while doing all the evil they can (vv. 4-5).

In Josiah's days God contrasts two sisters: faithless Israel, whom he divorced and exiled, and treacherous Judah, who watched it happen, did the same, and returned only in pretence (vv. 6-10). So Israel is judged the more righteous of the two (v. 11), and the call goes north: Return, faithless Israel, on one condition — Only acknowledge your guilt (vv. 12-13).
