verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Oh That My Head Were Waters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people! (v. 1). And in the same breath, Oh that I had in the desert a travelers' lodging place, that I might leave my people (v. 2). They bend their tongues like bows and do not know me (v. 3); no neighbour can be trusted and every brother is a deceiver (vv. 4-5); they refuse to know me (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet weeps for his people and longs to escape them at once, and the sin he grieves is a collapse of truth between neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people! Oh that I had in the desert a travelers' lodging place, that I might leave my people and go away from them! For they are all adulterers, a company of treacherous men. They bend their tongue like a bow; falsehood and not truth has grown strong in the land; for they proceed from evil to evil, and they do not know me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!

This is the verse that gave Jeremiah his title. The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible it is the last verse of chapter 8, which fits: it is the answer to the balm of Gilead. There is no cure, so there are tears.

And notice the scale he wants. Not a few tears but a head turned to water, eyes become a spring that never runs dry, weeping day and night. He is saying that the grief he already feels is inadequate to what he is looking at.

The psalmist knew the same tears: My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law (Ps 119:136). Paul knew them for his own nation: I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart (Rom 9:2). And on the last approach to Jerusalem, when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it (Luke 19:41). Christ stood where Jeremiah stood, looked at the same city, and cried.

It is a fair question whether any of us weep over anything but our own losses.

Oh that I had in the desert a travelers' lodging place, that I might leave my people and go away from them! For they are all adulterers, a company of treacherous men.

And then, immediately, the opposite wish. Give me a shack in the desert, a rest house on a caravan road, anywhere away from these people. The ESV notes this is 9:1 in the Hebrew, so the two verses belong tightly together.

The same man wants to weep for them and to be rid of them. Anyone who has loved a difficult family, church or city recognises both, often in one afternoon. Scripture does not tidy the prophet's emotions into consistency.

They bend their tongue like a bow; falsehood and not truth has grown strong in the land; for they proceed from evil to evil, and they do not know me, declares the LORD.

A bow is drawn deliberately, aimed, and released to wound at a distance. That is the tongue here: not careless talk but weaponised speech. The ESV notes an alternative reading of the middle clause; either way, falsehood has become the strong thing in the land, the force everything else bends around.

And the root is named last: they do not know me. Not, they do not know about me.

verseByVerse.quote: Let everyone beware of his neighbor, and put no trust in any brother, for every brother is a deceiver, and every neighbor goes about as a slanderer. Everyone deceives his neighbor, and no one speaks the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies; they weary themselves committing iniquity. Heaping oppression upon oppression, and deceit upon deceit, they refuse to know me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let everyone beware of his neighbor, and put no trust in any brother, for every brother is a deceiver, and every neighbor goes about as a slanderer.

This is what a society looks like when truth has collapsed: a standing instruction to trust nobody. Not enemies — neighbor and brother. The people you live beside and the people you are related to.

Trust is the invisible infrastructure of ordinary life. When it goes, everything costs more: every agreement needs a lawyer, every statement needs verification, every relationship carries a guard. The verse describes a nation living that way, and it is describing the fruit of the lying they were so proud of.

Everyone deceives his neighbor, and no one speaks the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies; they weary themselves committing iniquity.

Two phrases repay attention. They have taught their tongue to speak lies: this is trained behaviour, practised until it is fluent. Nobody starts as an accomplished liar; it is learned, and the learning is done by repetition.

And they weary themselves committing iniquity. Sin is hard work. Keeping the accounts straight, remembering what was said to whom, maintaining the version of yourself that different people are shown: it is exhausting, and the exhaustion is invisible from outside. The gospel's offer of rest lands precisely here.

Heaping oppression upon oppression, and deceit upon deceit, they refuse to know me, declares the LORD.

Refuse to know me. The second time in four verses. Ignorance of God in this book is not a gap in education; it is a decision maintained daily, and it is the reason the neighbours cannot trust each other.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — I Will Refine Them and Test Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do, because of my people? (v. 7). Their tongue is a deadly arrow, speaking peace and planning ambush (v. 8), and the refrain returns: Shall I not punish them for these things? (v. 9). God takes up weeping for the emptied pastures (v. 10) and will make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals (v. 11). Why is the land ruined? Because they have forsaken my law and followed the Baals (vv. 12-14), so they will eat bitter food and be scattered (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the judgment is refining work, and its cause is stated plainly so that no one need guess.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do, because of my people? Their tongue is a deadly arrow; it speaks deceitfully; with his mouth each speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he plans an ambush for him. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do, because of my people?

The refining image returns from chapter 6, where the assay failed. But listen to the middle of the sentence: for what else can I do, because of my people?

That is the language of a parent at the end of the options, and it is astonishing on the lips of God. He is not confessing weakness; he is showing the reader what this has cost him. Judgment here is not the first thing tried. It is what remains after persistent prophets, warnings, droughts and mercies have all been refused.

Their tongue is a deadly arrow; it speaks deceitfully; with his mouth each speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he plans an ambush for him.

The arrow again, and now the exact mechanism: speaks peace aloud, plans an ambush inwardly. This is the sin of the double heart — friendliness as cover. Every office and every congregation knows the pattern, and the damage is worse than open hostility because the victim never sees it coming.

Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?

The refrain of 5:9 and 5:29 once more. A God who watched neighbours ambush one another and shrugged would not be kind.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will take up weeping and wailing for the mountains, and a lamentation for the pastures of the wilderness, because they are laid waste so that no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard; both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled and are gone. I will make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals, and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant." Who is the man so wise that he can understand this? To whom has the mouth of the LORD spoken, that he may declare it? Why is the land ruined and laid waste like a wilderness, so that no one passes through? And the LORD says: "Because they have forsaken my law that I set before them, and have not obeyed my voice or walked in accord with it, but have stubbornly followed their own hearts and have gone after the Baals, as their fathers taught them. Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed this people with bitter food, and give them poisonous water to drink. I will scatter them among the nations whom neither they nor their fathers have known, and I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will take up weeping and wailing for the mountains, and a lamentation for the pastures of the wilderness, because they are laid waste so that no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard; both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled and are gone.

Now it is God who weeps. Jeremiah wanted a head of waters in verse 1; here the LORD takes up the lament himself, and it is for the countryside: empty pastures, no cattle lowing, birds gone, roads with nobody on them.

Whatever else is true of the judgment in this book, it is not the act of a God who feels nothing. He grieves the loss of his own creation, and he says so before it happens.

I will make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals, and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant."

Jackals move in when people move out. The city of David becomes a den for scavengers.

Who is the man so wise that he can understand this? To whom has the mouth of the LORD spoken, that he may declare it? Why is the land ruined and laid waste like a wilderness, so that no one passes through?

The question that gets asked after every catastrophe: why? And God does not leave it to be guessed at, argued over or turned into philosophy. He answers it himself, in plain words, immediately.

And the LORD says: "Because they have forsaken my law that I set before them, and have not obeyed my voice or walked in accord with it, but have stubbornly followed their own hearts and have gone after the Baals, as their fathers taught them.

Four verbs of the same movement: forsaken, not obeyed, not walked, followed their own hearts. And the last phrase adds the transmission: as their fathers taught them. Idolatry is handed down like a trade. What a generation practises casually, the next inherits as normal, and the chain has to be broken by somebody or it runs.

Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed this people with bitter food, and give them poisonous water to drink. I will scatter them among the nations whom neither they nor their fathers have known, and I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them."

Bitter food, poisoned water, scattering: the diet and the address of exile. And the phrase whom neither they nor their fathers have known makes the loneliness of it concrete — strangers, foreign speech, no family memory of the place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Call for the Mourning Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Consider, and call for the mourning women to come, to raise a wailing until every eye runs with tears (vv. 17-18). The sound of wailing is heard from Zion (v. 19), and women are told to teach their daughters a lament (v. 20), For death has come up into our windows; it has entered our palaces, cutting off the children from the streets (v. 21). Bodies will fall like sheaves after the reaper, and none shall gather them (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief on this scale needs professionals and a curriculum: a generation must be taught how to mourn.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Consider, and call for the mourning women to come; send for the skillful women to come; let them make haste and raise a wailing over us, that our eyes may run down with tears and our eyelids flow with water. For a sound of wailing is heard from Zion: 'How we are ruined! We are utterly shamed, because we have left the land, because they have cast down our dwellings.'" Hear, O women, the word of the LORD, and let your ear receive the word of his mouth; teach to your daughters a lament, and each to her neighbor a dirge. For death has come up into our windows; it has entered our palaces, cutting off the children from the streets and the young men from the squares. Speak: "Thus declares the LORD, 'The dead bodies of men shall fall like dung upon the open field, like sheaves after the reaper, and none shall gather them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Consider, and call for the mourning women to come; send for the skillful women to come; let them make haste and raise a wailing over us, that our eyes may run down with tears and our eyelids flow with water.

Professional mourners were a real institution: skilled women who led the wailing at a funeral and drew the grief out of a family that could not find it alone. God says: send for them, and hurry.

The purpose is stated plainly — that our eyes may run down with tears. This is a people who need help to cry. Numbness is its own symptom, and there are seasons when the most honest thing a church can do is teach its people to lament rather than hurry them past it.

For a sound of wailing is heard from Zion: 'How we are ruined! We are utterly shamed, because we have left the land, because they have cast down our dwellings.'"

The lament is quoted before the event, as though from the far side of it: the land left, the houses pulled down. Exile spoken of in the past tense while the city still stands.

Hear, O women, the word of the LORD, and let your ear receive the word of his mouth; teach to your daughters a lament, and each to her neighbor a dirge.

Now the mourning becomes a curriculum: teach to your daughters a lament. It is a devastating picture of what is coming — grief that will last long enough that the next generation will need to know the songs.

For death has come up into our windows; it has entered our palaces, cutting off the children from the streets and the young men from the squares.

Death is pictured as a burglar climbing in at the window. Doors can be barred; windows were where a thief got in. And it takes the children from the streets and the young men from the squares — exactly the places where a healthy town makes its noise. The silence of 7:34 arrives.

Speak: "Thus declares the LORD, 'The dead bodies of men shall fall like dung upon the open field, like sheaves after the reaper, and none shall gather them.'"

A harvest image turned inside out. Behind the reaper the sheaves lie in rows, waiting to be gathered — and no one comes. It is the picture of 8:20 completed: the harvest that was past is now a harvest of the dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — Let Him Who Boasts Boast in This
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches (v. 23), but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight (v. 24). The days are coming when God will punish all who are circumcised merely in the flesh (v. 25), for the nations are uncircumcised and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Against a chapter of ruin stands the one thing worth having: knowing the God who delights in steadfast love, justice and righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the LORD." "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will punish all those who are circumcised merely in the flesh— Egypt, Judah, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and all who dwell in the desert who cut the corners of their hair, for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches,

After sixteen verses of ruin, the chapter turns, and what it offers is the most quoted passage in the book after the new covenant. Three boasts are forbidden, and they are the three things human beings have always traded on: brains, strength and money.

They are still the three. Qualifications, capability, security. None of them is condemned as a possession; the wise man is not told to become stupid or the rich man to become poor. It is the boasting that is forbidden — resting your identity and your confidence there.

And all three failed in this chapter. The wise men were put to shame (8:9), the mighty could not hold the wall, and the rich lost their fields to conquerors (8:10).

but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the LORD."

One boast is permitted, and it is not an achievement: that he understands and knows me. The whole chapter has said twice that they do not know me and refuse to know me; here is the cure, offered as the one thing worth being proud of.

And notice what is to be known — not raw power, but character: steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. God delights in those three, which means they are the three his people should practise. Micah put the same list as a command (Mic 6:8); here it is a description of God himself.

Paul quotes this verse twice, both times in shortened form: Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (1 Cor 1:31; 2 Cor 10:17). He uses it in a letter to a church obsessed with clever speakers, powerful personalities and money — the same three boasts, in a Greek city, six centuries later.

Ask it personally. If the three were removed — the competence, the strength, the security — what would be left to say about yourself? Verse 24 offers the only answer that survives the removal.

"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will punish all those who are circumcised merely in the flesh— Egypt, Judah, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and all who dwell in the desert who cut the corners of their hair, for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart."

The chapter ends by putting Judah in a list with Egypt, Edom, Ammon and Moab. Several of those nations practised circumcision as a custom; Judah had it as a covenant sign. God says that at the level that matters they are indistinguishable, because Israel is uncircumcised in heart.

It is the theme of 4:4 and 6:10 brought to its conclusion, and Paul draws the line straight through to the church: circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Rom 2:29). Every external mark of belonging — baptism, membership, family faith, church attendance — sits under this verse. The mark is good. It settles nothing about the heart it is meant to signify.

9.title: Let Him Who Boasts Boast in This
9.overview:
Jeremiah wishes his head were water and his eyes a fountain of tears for his slaughtered people, and in the next breath wishes he could leave them altogether (vv. 1-2). Tongues are bent like bows, falsehood has grown strong, and no neighbour or brother can be trusted; they have trained their tongues to lie, wearying themselves with iniquity, and they refuse to know God (vv. 3-6).

God will refine and test them, for what else can I do (v. 7); their tongues speak peace and plan ambush (vv. 8-9). He takes up weeping for the emptied pastures and will make Jerusalem a lair of jackals (vv. 10-11). Why is the land ruined? Because they forsook his law and followed the Baals as their fathers taught them, so they will eat bitter food and be scattered (vv. 12-16).

Mourning women are summoned to teach a weeping the people cannot manage alone, and daughters are to be taught laments, for death has climbed in at the windows and the dead lie like ungathered sheaves (vv. 17-22). Then the turn: let no one boast in wisdom, might or riches, but only in knowing the LORD who practises steadfast love, justice and righteousness (vv. 23-24). And the days are coming when all who are circumcised merely in the flesh will be punished, for Israel too is uncircumcised in heart (vv. 25-26).
9.theology:
Grief over sin is a mark of the faithful, and it is shared by God himself (vv. 1, 10; Ps 119:136; Rom 9:2; Luke 19:41). Refusing to know God (vv. 3, 6) destroys trust between neighbours, and sin is exhausting labour (v. 5).

Judgment is what remains when every mercy has been refused — what else can I do (v. 7) — and its cause is stated plainly rather than left to speculation (vv. 12-14). Idolatry is transmitted by teaching (v. 14).

The one permitted boast is knowing God, whose delight is in steadfast love, justice and righteousness (vv. 23-24; Mic 6:8), quoted by Paul against boasting in wisdom, power and wealth (1 Cor 1:31; 2 Cor 10:17). External covenant marks settle nothing without a circumcised heart (vv. 25-26; 4:4; Rom 2:29).
9.examples:
Wanting to weep for people and to be rid of them on the same afternoon.

A tongue drawn, aimed and released like a bow.

Trust as the invisible infrastructure that makes ordinary life cheap.

Friendliness used as cover for an ambush.

Teaching your daughters the songs because the grief will outlast you.

Brains, strength and money: what is left if all three are removed?

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Hear the word that the LORD speaks to you, O house of Israel.<sup>2</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Learn not the way of the nations, nor be dismayed at the signs of the heavens because the nations are dismayed at them,<sup>3</sup>for the customs of the peoples are vanity. A tree from the forest is cut down and worked with an axe by the hands of a craftsman.<sup>4</sup>They decorate it with silver and gold; they fasten it with hammer and nails so that it cannot move.<sup>5</sup>Their idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, and they cannot speak; they have to be carried, for they cannot walk. Do not be afraid of them, for they cannot do evil, neither is it in them to do good."<sup>6</sup>There is none like you, O LORD; you are great, and your name is great in might.<sup>7</sup>Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? For this is your due; for among all the wise ones of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is none like you.<sup>8</sup>They are both stupid and foolish; the instruction of idols is but wood!<sup>9</sup>Beaten silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz. They are the work of the craftsman and of the hands of the goldsmith; their clothing is violet and purple; they are all the work of skilled men.<sup>10</sup>But the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King. At his wrath the earth quakes, and the nations cannot endure his indignation.<sup>11</sup>Thus shall you say to them: "The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from under the heavens."<sup>12</sup>It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens.<sup>13</sup>When he utters his voice, there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.<sup>14</sup>Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them.<sup>15</sup>They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish.<sup>16</sup>Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.<sup>17</sup>Gather up your bundle from the ground, O you who dwell under siege!<sup>18</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I am slinging out the inhabitants of the land at this time, and I will bring distress on them, that they may feel it."<sup>19</sup>Woe is me because of my hurt! My wound is grievous. But I said, "Truly this is an affliction, and I must bear it."<sup>20</sup>My tent is destroyed, and all my cords are broken; my children have gone from me, and they are not; there is no one to spread my tent again and to set up my curtains.<sup>21</sup>For the shepherds are stupid and do not inquire of the LORD; therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered.<sup>22</sup>A voice, a rumor! Behold, it comes!— a great commotion out of the north country to make the cities of Judah a desolation, a lair of jackals.<sup>23</sup>I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps.<sup>24</sup>Correct me, O LORD, but in justice; not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing.<sup>25</sup>Pour out your wrath on the nations that know you not, and on the peoples that call not on your name, for they have devoured Jacob; they have devoured him and consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Learn Not the Way of the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Learn not the way of the nations, nor be dismayed at the signs of the heavens (vv. 1-2), for the customs of the peoples are vanity: a tree is felled, worked with an axe, plated with silver and gold and nailed down so that it cannot move (vv. 3-4). Their idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, and they cannot speak; they have to be carried, for they cannot walk. Do not be afraid of them, for they cannot do evil, neither is it in them to do good (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The gods of the nations have to be nailed upright and carried home; they can neither harm you nor help you.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word that the LORD speaks to you, O house of Israel. Thus says the LORD: "Learn not the way of the nations, nor be dismayed at the signs of the heavens because the nations are dismayed at them, for the customs of the peoples are vanity. A tree from the forest is cut down and worked with an axe by the hands of a craftsman. They decorate it with silver and gold; they fasten it with hammer and nails so that it cannot move. Their idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, and they cannot speak; they have to be carried, for they cannot walk. Do not be afraid of them, for they cannot do evil, neither is it in them to do good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear the word that the LORD speaks to you, O house of Israel. Thus says the LORD: "Learn not the way of the nations, nor be dismayed at the signs of the heavens because the nations are dismayed at them,

The danger named here is imitation. Learn not the way of the nations — not their crimes first, but their way: the assumptions everyone around you holds without examining them. And the specific example is fear of the signs of the heavens: eclipses, comets, the movement of planets read as omens. The pagan world lived under the sky in dread.

The remedy God gives is not more information about astronomy. It is that the heavens belong to him, so they carry no message of doom for his people. Every age has its version of dread, read off the charts and the headlines, and believers absorb it simply by breathing the air.

for the customs of the peoples are vanity. A tree from the forest is cut down and worked with an axe by the hands of a craftsman. They decorate it with silver and gold; they fasten it with hammer and nails so that it cannot move.

Now the satire, and it is done by simple narration. Follow the process: a tree is cut in the forest; a carpenter shapes it; a metalworker plates it; and finally it is nailed down so that it cannot move — because otherwise it would fall over. The ESV notes that vanity here may be rendered "vapor" or "mist": breath, the same word Ecclesiastes uses.

Isaiah told the joke at greater length: a man cuts a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner and warm himself, and out of the rest he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it, saying Deliver me, for you are my god! (Isa 44:15, 17). The wood that cooked the meal becomes the deity.

Their idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, and they cannot speak; they have to be carried, for they cannot walk. Do not be afraid of them, for they cannot do evil, neither is it in them to do good."

The image is perfect and slightly comic: a scarecrow in a vegetable patch. Upright, human-shaped, dressed, motionless, and frightening only to birds. The ESV notes that they in this verse is the Hebrew's own word choice, keeping the idols firmly in the plural and impersonal.

Three disabilities: cannot speak, cannot walk, must be carried. A god you have to transport is not a god. The psalm makes the same list and adds the sting: Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps 115:8).

And then the conclusion, which is the reason the passage exists: Do not be afraid of them. Israel was tempted to worship these things partly out of fear that they might be real. God's answer is that they cannot hurt you and cannot help you, which is the most dismissive sentence anyone ever wrote about a religion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–16 — There Is None Like You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is none like you, O LORD; you are great, and your name is great in might (vv. 6-7). Idols are wood dressed in silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz, the work of skilled men (vv. 8-9). But the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King (v. 10), and the gods who did not make heaven and earth will perish (v. 11). He made the earth by his power, sends the rain, lightning and wind (vv. 12-13), while every goldsmith is shamed by his images, in which there is no breath (vv. 14-15). Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The satire turns into a hymn: the maker of the world against the things that had to be made.

verseByVerse.quote: There is none like you, O LORD; you are great, and your name is great in might. Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? For this is your due; for among all the wise ones of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is none like you. They are both stupid and foolish; the instruction of idols is but wood! Beaten silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz. They are the work of the craftsman and of the hands of the goldsmith; their clothing is violet and purple; they are all the work of skilled men. But the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King. At his wrath the earth quakes, and the nations cannot endure his indignation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is none like you, O LORD; you are great, and your name is great in might. Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? For this is your due; for among all the wise ones of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is none like you.

In the middle of the satire, worship breaks out. This is how the Bible argues: not only by exposing the counterfeit but by displaying the real thing. Set beside a nailed-down scarecrow, the living God needs no argument, only description.

Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? The question assumes an obvious answer and the whole book is the evidence that people manage it anyway. And note the title: King of the nations, not only of Judah. The peoples who bow to blocks of wood are already his subjects.

They are both stupid and foolish; the instruction of idols is but wood! Beaten silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz. They are the work of the craftsman and of the hands of the goldsmith; their clothing is violet and purple; they are all the work of skilled men.

The instruction of idols is but wood. Whatever teaching comes from them amounts to timber. And the inventory of expense is deliberate: silver shipped from Tarshish, gold from Uphaz, violet and purple cloth, skilled craftsmen. Enormous investment, real artistry, imported materials — and the finished product still has to be carried.

Modern idols are also expensive, beautifully made and widely admired. Cost and craftsmanship have never been evidence of divinity.

But the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King. At his wrath the earth quakes, and the nations cannot endure his indignation.

Three titles in one line: the true God, against the false; the living God, against things with no breath in them; the everlasting King, against gods that will perish. This is the sentence the chapter is built around.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus shall you say to them: "The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from under the heavens." It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice, there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses. Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish. Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus shall you say to them: "The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from under the heavens."

The ESV notes something remarkable about this verse: it is in Aramaic, not Hebrew — the only such verse in the book. Aramaic was the international language, the speech of diplomacy and trade. So here is a sentence God gives his people to say to the nations, in the nations' own language.

The test it applies is creation. Did your god make this? If not, he is a creature at best and a piece of furniture at worst, and he will not outlast the world he did not make.

It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice, there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.

Power, wisdom, understanding — and then weather. Thunder is his voice; mist rises at his command; lightning and rain arrive together; and the wind is kept in storehouses, as if God had a barn for gales. The people were tempted to worship storm gods. Jeremiah says the storm runs errands for the LORD.

Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish.

There is no breath in them is the decisive charge. In Genesis God breathed into man and he became a living creature; here men breathe over their gods and nothing happens. The direction of life runs one way only.

Paul argued the same way in Athens: we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man (Acts 17:29). And to Corinth: an idol has no real existence, for there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things (1 Cor 8:4, 6).

Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.

The comparison ends with relationship rather than argument. God is the portion of Jacob — the share, the inheritance, what the family actually owns. And, astonishingly, the possession runs both ways: Israel is his inheritance. The idol-worshipper owns an object. The believer is owned by, and owns, a person.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gather up your bundle from the ground, O you who dwell under siege! (v. 17), for God is slinging out the inhabitants of the land (v. 18). A voice mourns: My wound is grievous, the tent destroyed, the cords broken, the children gone and no one left to pitch it again (vv. 19-20). The shepherds did not inquire of the LORD, so the flock is scattered (v. 21), and a great commotion comes out of the north (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Exile packed into a bundle, a home that cannot be put up again, and shepherds who never asked God anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Gather up your bundle from the ground, O you who dwell under siege! For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I am slinging out the inhabitants of the land at this time, and I will bring distress on them, that they may feel it." Woe is me because of my hurt! My wound is grievous. But I said, "Truly this is an affliction, and I must bear it." My tent is destroyed, and all my cords are broken; my children have gone from me, and they are not; there is no one to spread my tent again and to set up my curtains. For the shepherds are stupid and do not inquire of the LORD; therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered. A voice, a rumor! Behold, it comes!— a great commotion out of the north country to make the cities of Judah a desolation, a lair of jackals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gather up your bundle from the ground, O you who dwell under siege!

From hymn to evacuation in one line. Gather up your bundle is what a refugee does: everything you own on the floor, and you take what you can carry. The whole life of a household reduced to a pack.

For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I am slinging out the inhabitants of the land at this time, and I will bring distress on them, that they may feel it."

The picture is a sling: stones whirled and flung far away. And the purpose clause is almost gentle in its severity: that they may feel it. A people who did not feel the earlier blows (5:3) will feel this one. Pain is being used to restore sensation.

Woe is me because of my hurt! My wound is grievous. But I said, "Truly this is an affliction, and I must bear it."

Who speaks here? The prophet and the people are hard to separate, which is the point: he carries their grief as his own (8:21). And the response is neither denial nor collapse: this is an affliction, and I must bear it. There is a kind of faith that consists simply in shouldering what cannot be changed, without pretending it is light.

My tent is destroyed, and all my cords are broken; my children have gone from me, and they are not; there is no one to spread my tent again and to set up my curtains.

The nation pictured as a tent: poles down, guy ropes snapped, and — the line that stops you — my children have gone from me, and they are not. Worst of all, no one is left to help put it back up. That is exile: not only loss but the loss of the hands that would have rebuilt.

For the shepherds are stupid and do not inquire of the LORD; therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered. A voice, a rumor! Behold, it comes!— a great commotion out of the north country to make the cities of Judah a desolation, a lair of jackals.

The leaders again (2:8), and the charge is precise: they do not inquire of the LORD. Not that they consulted him and disobeyed, but that it never occurred to them to ask. Leadership that does not ask God anything will scatter the people it is meant to gather. Chapter 23 will return to these shepherds with a promise of a better one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–25 — The Way of Man Is Not in Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps (v. 23). So: Correct me, O LORD, but in justice; not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing (v. 24). And a prayer that God's wrath fall on the nations that devoured Jacob and do not call on his name (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet who has watched a nation steer itself into ruin asks for correction rather than for exemption.

verseByVerse.quote: I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps. Correct me, O LORD, but in justice; not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing. Pour out your wrath on the nations that know you not, and on the peoples that call not on your name, for they have devoured Jacob; they have devoured him and consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps.

After watching a nation navigate itself into catastrophe, the prophet states the lesson as a confession. Human beings are not self-directing. We can choose, plan and walk, and we cannot finally set the course of a life. Proverbs says it without the ruins in view: The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (Prov 16:9). The psalm says it warmly: The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when he delights in his way (Ps 37:23).

This is either the most frightening sentence in the chapter or the most freeing, depending on who is holding the map.

Correct me, O LORD, but in justice; not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing.

Notice what he asks for. Not exemption from correction — correct me — but measure in it. He has just watched what unrestrained judgment looks like, and he asks to be dealt with in justice rather than in wrath.

A believer can pray this honestly. O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger (Ps 6:1). And the New Testament gives the answer the prophet could not yet see: God disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10). For those in Christ the correction is never the anger; the anger fell elsewhere.

Pour out your wrath on the nations that know you not, and on the peoples that call not on your name, for they have devoured Jacob; they have devoured him and consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.

The chapter ends with a hard prayer, and it is honest about what the invaders did. God used Babylon, and Babylon will answer for how it behaved — the last chapters of this book are given to exactly that. Being an instrument in God's hand is no defence for cruelty.

10.title: Scarecrows in a Cucumber Field
10.overview:
Israel is told not to learn the way of the nations or to dread the signs of the heavens, because the customs of the peoples are vapour: a tree is cut, carved, plated with silver and gold, and nailed upright so it cannot fall (vv. 1-4). Idols are scarecrows in a cucumber field — they cannot speak or walk, must be carried, and can do neither harm nor good (v. 5).

Against them stands the LORD: There is none like you, King of the nations (vv. 6-7). Idols are wood dressed in imported silver and gold by skilled men (vv. 8-9), but the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King (v. 10). In Aramaic, the language of the nations, Israel is to tell them that gods who did not make heaven and earth will perish (v. 11). He made the world, and thunder, mist, lightning and wind are his (vv. 12-13); images have no breath in them (vv. 14-15); and he is the portion of Jacob (v. 16).

Then the siege: gather your bundle, for God is slinging out the inhabitants that they may feel it (vv. 17-18). A voice mourns a grievous wound, a tent with broken cords and children gone, with no one left to pitch it again (vv. 19-20). The shepherds never inquired of the LORD, so the flock is scattered, and a commotion comes from the north (vv. 21-22). Jeremiah confesses that man cannot direct his own steps, asks to be corrected in justice rather than anger, and prays against the nations that devoured Jacob (vv. 23-25).
10.theology:
Idolatry is exposed by narration: gods that must be manufactured, fastened upright and carried are neither to be feared nor trusted (vv. 3-5; Ps 115:4-8; Isa 44:14-17; Acts 17:29; 1 Cor 8:4-6). Believers absorb the fears of their culture unless taught otherwise (v. 2).

The living God is known as Creator, and creation is the test he gives the nations (vv. 11-13; Rev 4:11). He is his people's portion, and they are his inheritance (v. 16).

Human beings cannot direct their own steps (v. 23; Prov 16:9). The right prayer is for correction in justice, not for exemption (v. 24; Ps 6:1), and for those in Christ discipline is never wrath (Heb 12:10). Instruments of God's judgment remain accountable for their cruelty (v. 25).
10.examples:
A god that has to be nailed down so it will not topple over.

A scarecrow in a vegetable patch: upright, dressed, and frightening only to birds.

Wood that cooked the dinner, carved into a deity.

Storms running errands for the God some people worship as a storm.

A household reduced to what one person can carry.

Leaders to whom it never occurred to ask God anything.

They have gone after other gods to serve them. Though they cry to me, I will not listen to them.<sup>12</sup>Then the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they make offerings, but they cannot save them in the time of their trouble.<sup>13</sup>For your gods have become as many as your cities, O Judah, and as many as the streets of Jerusalem are the altars you have set up to shame, altars to make offerings to Baal.<sup>14</sup>"Therefore do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer on their behalf, for I will not listen when they call to me in the time of their trouble.<sup>15</sup>What right has my beloved in my house, when she has done many vile deeds? Can even sacrificial flesh avert your doom? Can you then exult?<sup>16</sup>The LORD once called you 'a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit.' But with the roar of a great tempest he will set fire to it, and its branches will be consumed.<sup>17</sup>The LORD of hosts, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you, because of the evil that the house of Israel and the house of Judah have done, provoking me to anger by making offerings to Baal."<sup>18</sup>The LORD made it known to me and I knew; then you showed me their deeds.<sup>19</sup>But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes, saying, "Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name be remembered no more."<sup>20</sup>But, O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause.<sup>21</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, and say, "Do not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand"—<sup>22</sup>therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will punish them. The young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine,<sup>23</sup>and none of them shall be left. For I will bring disaster upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their punishment."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Hear the Words of This Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is sent to preach the covenant: Cursed be the man who does not hear the words of this covenant (vv. 1-3), given when God brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, with its promise, So shall you be my people, and I will be your God (v. 4) and its oath of a land flowing with milk and honey, to which the prophet answers, So be it, LORD (v. 5). He is to proclaim it in the streets (v. 6), for God warned their fathers persistently, even to this day (v. 7), and they did not obey (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant came with blessing and curse attached, and the prophet says amen to both before preaching either.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Cursed be the man who does not hear the words of this covenant that I commanded your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying, Listen to my voice, and do all that I command you. So shall you be my people, and I will be your God, that I may confirm the oath that I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as at this day." Then I answered, "So be it, LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Cursed be the man who does not hear the words of this covenant

This chapter is a covenant lawsuit, and it opens by reading the contract aloud. The sentence Jeremiah must announce is one of the curses from Deuteronomy, where the whole nation said amen to it: Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them. And all the people shall say, 'Amen' (Deut 27:26).

Judah had agreed to the terms. That is the force of everything that follows. God is not imposing something new; he is enforcing what they swore.

that I commanded your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying, Listen to my voice, and do all that I command you. So shall you be my people, and I will be your God,

Two things stand together here. The iron furnace is Egypt: a smelting oven, the place of heat and slavery from which God dragged them. Rescue came first. Then the terms: Listen to my voice, and do all that I command you. Obedience is the response to redemption, never the price of it.

And at the centre, the sentence that runs through the whole Bible: So shall you be my people, and I will be your God. That is what a covenant is for. It appears again at the heart of the new covenant in chapter 31, and again at the end of Revelation. The relationship is the point; the commandments describe what it looks like.

that I may confirm the oath that I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as at this day." Then I answered, "So be it, LORD."

Jeremiah's reply is one word in Hebrew liturgy: amen. So be it, LORD. He is standing where Israel stood at the foot of the mountain, agreeing to a covenant that carries a curse, and he says amen to it before he preaches a syllable of it.

That is what makes him able to preach judgment without cruelty. He has said amen to the terms himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem: Hear the words of this covenant and do them. For I solemnly warned your fathers when I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, warning them persistently, even to this day, saying, Obey my voice. Yet they did not obey or incline their ear, but everyone walked in the stubbornness of his evil heart. Therefore I brought upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do, but they did not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD said to me, "Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem: Hear the words of this covenant and do them.

The covenant is not to be read in the temple to the devout but shouted in the streets of the towns. Hear and do them: in this book hearing is never complete until it produces action.

For I solemnly warned your fathers when I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, warning them persistently, even to this day, saying, Obey my voice.

Persistently, even to this day. The warning has been continuous for the whole history of the nation, which is God's patience described as a long, unbroken sentence. Nobody will be able to say the terms were unclear.

Yet they did not obey or incline their ear, but everyone walked in the stubbornness of his evil heart. Therefore I brought upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do, but they did not."

Read the last sentence slowly, because it is precise. God brought on them all the words of this covenant — the very words they had agreed to. The disaster is not an outburst; it is the contract being honoured. God keeps his word in judgment as faithfully as in blessing, and that is a strange comfort: a God whose promises hold is a God whose warnings hold too.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A conspiracy exists among the men of Judah (v. 9): they have returned to their forefathers' iniquities and broken the covenant (v. 10). So God brings disaster that they cannot escape, and will not listen to their cry (v. 11); they will call on the gods to whom they burn offerings, but they cannot save them in the time of their trouble (v. 12), for their gods are as many as their cities (v. 13). And again: do not pray for this people (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry has become organised, and the gods multiplied for every street cannot answer a single emergency.

verseByVerse.quote: Again the LORD said to me, "A conspiracy exists among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, who refused to hear my words. They have gone after other gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant that I made with their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again the LORD said to me, "A conspiracy exists among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

A conspiracy is organised, agreed and quiet. God is not describing scattered individuals slipping into sin but a settled arrangement among the leading men of the nation to go their own way while keeping the appearances.

Sin usually becomes respectable by consensus. Once everyone who matters is doing it, it stops feeling like rebellion and starts feeling like realism.

They have turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, who refused to hear my words. They have gone after other gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant that I made with their fathers.

Turned back — this is not innovation but reversion. Josiah's reform had pushed the idols out of sight; the moment the pressure eased they came back, because the heart had never changed. Reformation that is imposed from above always has this fragility, and it is why the promise of chapter 31 has to be about hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, thus says the LORD, Behold, I am bringing disaster upon them that they cannot escape. Though they cry to me, I will not listen to them. Then the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they make offerings, but they cannot save them in the time of their trouble. For your gods have become as many as your cities, O Judah, and as many as the streets of Jerusalem are the altars you have set up to shame, altars to make offerings to Baal. "Therefore do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer on their behalf, for I will not listen when they call to me in the time of their trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, thus says the LORD, Behold, I am bringing disaster upon them that they cannot escape. Though they cry to me, I will not listen to them.

Two terrible phrases: that they cannot escape, and Though they cry to me, I will not listen. This is not God refusing a repentant sinner; it is God refusing a nation that has cried out in every emergency for generations while serving other gods in between. Prayer offered as a fire extinguisher, by people who want rescue but not God, is not prayer.

Then the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they make offerings, but they cannot save them in the time of their trouble.

So they will try the other gods, the ones they have been funding all along. And the verdict on them is the quiet, devastating they cannot save them in the time of their trouble. Every substitute god is fine until there is trouble. That is what trouble is for, in the mercy of God: it shows which of the things we serve can act.

For your gods have become as many as your cities, O Judah, and as many as the streets of Jerusalem are the altars you have set up to shame, altars to make offerings to Baal.

A god for every town and an altar on every street — the line from 2:28 repeated with the streets added. Idolatry multiplies because no single idol ever delivers, so another is added, and another.

"Therefore do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer on their behalf, for I will not listen when they call to me in the time of their trouble.

The prohibition of 7:16 returns, and it will come a third time (14:11). The repetition tells us Jeremiah kept praying — a man forbidden to intercede who could not stop.

It bears saying again what this is not. It is not a licence to write people off; no one but God can read another person's account. It is the most solemn warning Scripture gives about the point at which persistent refusal becomes settled, and the fact that it grieved the man commanded to obey it is part of the message.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What right has my beloved in my house, when she has done many vile deeds? Sacrificial flesh cannot avert the doom (v. 15). The LORD once called her a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit, but with the roar of a great tempest he will set it on fire (v. 16), for the planter himself has decreed disaster because of offerings made to Baal (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The one who planted the tree is the one who burns it; sacrifice offered by a faithless worshipper buys nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: What right has my beloved in my house, when she has done many vile deeds? Can even sacrificial flesh avert your doom? Can you then exult? The LORD once called you 'a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit.' But with the roar of a great tempest he will set fire to it, and its branches will be consumed. The LORD of hosts, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you, because of the evil that the house of Israel and the house of Judah have done, provoking me to anger by making offerings to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What right has my beloved in my house, when she has done many vile deeds? Can even sacrificial flesh avert your doom? Can you then exult?

The tone is that of a betrayed husband watching his wife arrive at his house with a gift. My beloved — the affection has not gone. And the questions are sharp: what business have you here, and do you imagine that meat on an altar will cancel this?

The answer the whole prophetic tradition gives is no. Sacrifice was never a payment that let the worshipper keep the sin. That is the difference between the gospel and religion: religion offers God something to buy space for what we love; the gospel takes the thing we love and kills it, and gives us God.

The LORD once called you 'a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit.' But with the roar of a great tempest he will set fire to it, and its branches will be consumed.

An olive tree lives for centuries and takes decades to come into full bearing; it is the picture of patient, long-term fruitfulness, and God says he once called them exactly that. The name was his, and it was warm.

Now the same tree is set alight in a storm. The tragedy is measured by what she was called: not a weed grubbed up, but a beautiful tree burned.

The LORD of hosts, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you, because of the evil that the house of Israel and the house of Judah have done, provoking me to anger by making offerings to Baal."

And the one who decrees the fire is the LORD of hosts, who planted you. He is not a stranger to the orchard. Everything that is lost here is his own work, which is why judgment costs God something.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — A Gentle Lamb Led to the Slaughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows Jeremiah what his neighbours are plotting (v. 18): But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, unaware of the scheme to cut him off from the land of the living (v. 19). He appeals to the LORD who tests the heart and the mind, committing his cause to him (v. 20). The plotters are the men of Anathoth, his own town, who tell him not to prophesy or die (v. 21), and God declares their punishment (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's own townsmen want him dead, and the words he uses about himself will be used of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD made it known to me and I knew; then you showed me their deeds. But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes, saying, "Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name be remembered no more." But, O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD made it known to me and I knew; then you showed me their deeds.

Now the chapter turns from the nation to the man, and this is the first of the passages usually called Jeremiah's confessions: his own prayers, complaints and terrors, preserved in the book. Here he learns something he did not know, and God is the one who tells him.

But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes, saying, "Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name be remembered no more."

He had been walking about among them entirely unsuspecting: a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, following the man with the rope, tame and trusting, with no idea where the path ends.

Their plan has three parts, and the third is the cruellest. Destroy the tree with its fruit, so nothing of his work survives. Cut him off from the land of the living. And that his name be remembered no more — erase him, so that it is as if he never spoke.

Isaiah had used the same picture of the servant of the LORD: like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7). It was the passage the Ethiopian was reading when Philip explained to him that it spoke of Jesus (Acts 8:32-33).

So Jeremiah's words about himself become, without his knowing it, a description of his Lord. The prophet was a lamb who did not know; Christ was the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29), and he knew exactly what was planned and walked into it anyway.

But, O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause.

This is how he handles it, and the last clause governs the rest: to you have I committed my cause. He does not organise a defence or repay them; he hands the case over.

The request for vengeance troubles Christian readers, and it should be read for what it is: a man refusing to take revenge and asking the righteous Judge to act instead. That is the opposite of personal retaliation, and it is the same instinct Peter records of Christ, who continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly. The God appealed to is the one who tests the heart and the mind (compare Ps 7:9; Rev 2:23) — which means Jeremiah is inviting a judgment that will examine him as well.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, and say, "Do not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand"— therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will punish them. The young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine, and none of them shall be left. For I will bring disaster upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their punishment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, and say, "Do not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand"—

And now the names. The men of Anathoth: his own village, three miles from Jerusalem, the priestly town where he grew up. These are the people who taught him, the families he knew, probably his own relatives — chapter 12 will say his brothers and his father's house dealt treacherously with him.

Their terms are simple: stop preaching or be killed. Not a theological argument, a threat.

It is the oldest pattern in Scripture. No prophet is acceptable in his hometown, said Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth, where they tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:24). He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). The hardest audience is usually the one that knew you as a child.

therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will punish them. The young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine, and none of them shall be left. For I will bring disaster upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their punishment."

God answers the threat against his servant personally, and the sentence includes a phrase that softens nothing: the year of their punishment. There is a date on it.

Two things to hold together from this chapter. Preaching the covenant faithfully made Jeremiah hated in his own village, and God took that hatred as aimed at himself. Anyone who has lost family or friends over their obedience to Christ is standing in a long line, and the Lord of hosts has noticed.

11.title: The Words of This Covenant
11.overview:
Jeremiah is sent to proclaim the covenant in the towns and streets: cursed is the man who will not hear its words, which God gave when he brought Israel out of the iron furnace of Egypt with the promise So shall you be my people, and I will be your God; the prophet answers So be it, LORD (vv. 1-6). God warned their fathers persistently and they did not obey, so he brought on them all the words of the covenant they had agreed to (vv. 7-8).

A conspiracy exists: they have reverted to their forefathers' idolatry and broken the covenant (vv. 9-10). So disaster comes that they cannot escape, and when they cry, God will not listen; the gods they funded cannot save them, being as many as their streets (vv. 11-13). Once more Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for them (v. 14).

Sacrificial meat will not avert the doom of a beloved who has done vile deeds (v. 15). The green olive tree God himself planted and named will be set alight (vv. 16-17). Then God reveals a plot: Jeremiah has been like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, unaware of men planning to cut him off and erase his name (vv. 18-19). He commits his cause to the God who tests hearts (v. 20). The plotters are the men of his own town, Anathoth, who threaten to kill him if he keeps preaching, and God declares the year of their punishment (vv. 21-23).
11.theology:
The covenant carried blessing and curse, and Judah had said amen to both (vv. 3-5; Deut 27:26; Deut 11:26-28; Gal 3:10). Rescue came before commands: obedience is the response to redemption (v. 4). Judgment here is God keeping his word, not losing his temper (v. 8).

Prayer used as an emergency service by people who serve other gods is not prayer (v. 11), and substitute gods fail precisely when trouble comes (v. 12). Sacrifice never buys permission to keep the sin (v. 15).

Jeremiah's words about himself — a gentle lamb led to the slaughter — describe Christ more truly than himself (v. 19; Isa 53:7; Acts 8:32; John 1:29). Faced with plots, he commits his cause to the God who tests the heart rather than taking revenge (v. 20), and his own townspeople are his fiercest opponents (vv. 21-23; Luke 4:24; John 1:11).
11.examples:
Saying amen to the terms before preaching a word of them.

Sin made respectable by consensus.

Reform imposed from above that lasts only while the pressure does.

Prayer used as a fire extinguisher.

A tree that takes decades to bear, burned in one storm.

The hardest audience: the people who knew you as a child.

Why do all who are treacherous thrive?<sup>2</sup>You plant them, and they take root; they grow and produce fruit; you are near in their mouth and far from their heart.<sup>3</sup>But you, O LORD, know me; you see me, and test my heart toward you.
