Let it come!"<sup>16</sup>I have not run away from being your shepherd, nor have I desired the day of sickness. You know what came out of my lips; it was before your face.<sup>17</sup>Be not a terror to me; you are my refuge in the day of disaster.<sup>18</sup>Let those be put to shame who persecute me, but let me not be put to shame; let them be dismayed, but let me not be dismayed; bring upon them the day of disaster; destroy them with double destruction!<sup>19</sup>Thus said the LORD to me: "Go and stand in the People's Gate, by which the kings of Judah enter and by which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem,<sup>20</sup>and say: 'Hear the word of the LORD, you kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who enter by these gates.<sup>21</sup>Thus says the LORD: Take care for the sake of your lives, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem.<sup>22</sup>And do not carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath or do any work, but keep the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers.<sup>23</sup>Yet they did not listen or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck, that they might not hear and receive instruction.<sup>24</sup>"'But if you listen to me, declares the LORD, and bring in no burden by the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, but keep the Sabbath day holy and do no work on it,<sup>25</sup>then there shall enter by the gates of this city kings and princes who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their officials, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And this city shall be inhabited forever.<sup>26</sup>And people shall come from the cities of Judah and the places around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the Shephelah, from the hill country, and from the Negeb, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and bringing thank offerings to the house of the LORD.<sup>27</sup>But if you do not listen to me, to keep the Sabbath day holy, and not to bear a burden and enter by the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, then I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem and shall not be quenched.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Sin Engraved on the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of their altars (v. 1), while their children remember the altars and Asherim on every hill (vv. 2-3). Their wealth will be spoil, and they will loosen their hand from the heritage God gave them and serve their enemies in an unknown land (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The record of sin is cut into the very place where God means to write his law.

verseByVerse.quote: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of their altars, while their children remember their altars and their Asherim, beside every green tree and on the high hills, on the mountains in the open country. Your wealth and all your treasures I will give for spoil as the price of your high places for sin throughout all your territory. You shall loosen your hand from your heritage that I gave to you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of their altars,

The image is of an inscription cut into stone with the hardest tools available: an iron stylus, a diamond point. Not written in ink, which fades, but engraved, which lasts.

And the surface it is cut into is the tablet of their heart. That phrase belongs to the covenant. God wrote his law on tablets of stone, and he had asked for it to be kept on the heart. What is engraved there instead is the record of their sin, so deep that it is now the grain of the wood rather than a stain on the surface.

Hold this verse beside the promise this book is moving toward: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (31:33). The new covenant is not a better set of rules but a different inscription on the same tablet — which requires the old one to be dealt with, and it was, at a cross.

The second surface is worse: the horns of their altars. The horns were where the blood of the sin offering was smeared, the place of atonement. Their sin is carved into the very furniture of forgiveness. Religion practised without repentance does not remove guilt; it records it.

while their children remember their altars and their Asherim, beside every green tree and on the high hills, on the mountains in the open country.

What the children remember is what the parents did. Not the Passover, not the law read at the feast, but where the shrines were and what happened there. The most reliable curriculum in any household is what the adults actually do.

Your wealth and all your treasures I will give for spoil as the price of your high places for sin throughout all your territory. You shall loosen your hand from your heritage that I gave to you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."

The sentence of 15:13-14 repeated, with one new phrase: You shall loosen your hand from your heritage. It is the picture of fingers being prised off something held tight. They will not hand the land over; it will be taken out of their grip.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD (v. 5): he is like a shrub in the desert in a salt land (v. 6). Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD (v. 7): He is like a tree planted by water, unafraid of heat, green in the year of drought, never ceasing to bear fruit (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Two lives are told as two plants, and the difference is not circumstance but where the roots go.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD. He is like a shrub in the desert, and shall not see any good come. He shall dwell in the parched places of the wilderness, in an uninhabited salt land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD.

Now one of the great passages of the book, and it is built as a pair of portraits. The first begins with Cursed, and the definition has three parts: he trusts in man, he makes flesh his strength, and his heart turns away from the LORD. The ESV notes that strength is in Hebrew "arm" — the muscle you lean on.

Notice that the three go together. Trusting human resources is not a neutral technique that happens to fail; it is a heart turning. Every reliance is a relationship.

This is not a warning against using doctors, savings or friends. It is about where the weight rests. The question is what you would still have if the arm you are leaning on gave way tomorrow.

He is like a shrub in the desert, and shall not see any good come. He shall dwell in the parched places of the wilderness, in an uninhabited salt land.

The picture is of scrub in the Judean wilderness: grey, stunted, alive in the technical sense. It is not that such a life collapses dramatically. It survives, and never flourishes. Shall not see any good come is almost worse than disaster — a life in which nothing good is ever quite noticed.

And an uninhabited salt land is soil where nothing will grow again, the ground around the Dead Sea. Misplaced trust does not only fail to feed you; it salts the field.

verseByVerse.quote: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD. He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD.

The second portrait, and the doubling is deliberate: he trusts in the LORD, and whose trust is the LORD. The object and the ground are the same person. He is not trusting God to deliver a particular outcome; God himself is the thing he is resting on.

He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit."

Psalm 1 has the same tree — like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season (Ps 1:3) — but Jeremiah adds the weather, and after chapter 14 we know why. The heat comes. The year of drought arrives. The point is not that the believer is exempt from the drought that scorched the whole country; it is that his roots are somewhere the drought does not reach.

Two words describe him in the crisis: he does not fear, and he is not anxious. Anyone who has tried to argue himself out of anxiety knows that this cannot be produced by effort. It is the fruit of where the roots are, and roots grow slowly, in ordinary weather, long before they are tested.

And the last clause is the one to sit with: it does not cease to bear fruit. Not merely survives; keeps producing, in the drought year, for other people's benefit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? (v. 9). God answers his own question: I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways (v. 10). Riches got unjustly leave a man a fool (v. 11). A glorious throne set on high from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary (v. 12), and those who forsake the LORD, the fountain of living water shall be put to shame (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody can read his own heart; God reads it, and the diagnosis drives us back to the fountain abandoned in chapter 2.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? "I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?

Here is the sentence that explains this entire book, and it should be taken a word at a time.

The heart — in Scripture not the emotions but the control centre of a person: mind, will and affections together, the part of you that decides. Deceitful above all things — it lies, and its most practised victim is its owner. Nothing else in creation is as good at it. Desperately sick — the word is used of an incurable wound, the kind that will not close.

Then the question, and it is not rhetorical despair: who can understand it? Not you, about yourself. That is the uncomfortable point. The instrument you would use to examine your heart is the heart, and it is the thing under suspicion. This is why sincerity is not a defence: a person can be entirely sincere and entirely deceived, because the deceiver lives inside.

"I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds."

The question is answered in the next breath, and the answer is God. I the LORD search the heart — the ESV notes that mind is in Hebrew "kidneys", the innermost parts. He does not guess at us from the outside; he reads what we cannot read.

That could be the most frightening sentence imaginable, and for the believer it is the opposite, because the God who reads it has dealt with what he finds. The right response is the psalmist's, and it takes courage: Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! (Ps 139:23).

And the diagnosis makes the promise later in this book necessary. A heart this sick cannot be managed, educated or resolved into health. It has to be replaced: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (31:33); I will give you a new heart (Ezek 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: Like the partridge that gathers a brood that she did not hatch, so is he who gets riches but not by justice; in the midst of his days they will leave him, and at his end he will be a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the partridge that gathers a brood that she did not hatch, so is he who gets riches but not by justice; in the midst of his days they will leave him, and at his end he will be a fool.

A single proverb dropped into the middle of the chapter, and it fits the theme: here is the heart's deceit working itself out in a bank account.

The picture is a bird sitting on eggs that are not hers. She keeps them warm, defends them, does all the work of a mother — and when they hatch they run off to their own kind. She is left with a bare nest and nothing to show for the sitting.

So with money gained unjustly. It looks like a clutch of eggs; the man broods over it; and in the midst of his days they will leave him. Not even at the end, when everyone's wealth departs, but halfway through, while he still had plans for it.

And the verdict is not that he is wicked, which he is, but that he is stupid: at his end he will be a fool. Injustice for profit is a bad investment.

verseByVerse.quote: A glorious throne set on high from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary. O LORD, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be put to shame; those who turn away from you shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A glorious throne set on high from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary.

After the wilderness scrub and the empty nest, worship. The temple is not first a building but a throne room, and it has been set on high from the beginning. Whatever happens to the city, that throne is not vacated.

O LORD, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be put to shame; those who turn away from you shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water.

Written in the earth is a striking phrase — names scratched in dust, which the next wind or footstep erases, in contrast to sin engraved with an iron pen in verse 1 and to the names written in heaven. The ESV notes that you here is in Hebrew "me", the prophet speaking of himself alongside God.

And the chapter reaches back to the book's first great image: they have forsaken the fountain of living water (2:13). Everything in between — the cisterns, the drought, the empty jars, the shrub in the salt land, the tree by the stream — has been about water, and here the source is named again.

Jesus stood in the temple courts at the feast of water-drawing and cried out, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. The fountain that Judah abandoned came to Jerusalem in person.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise (v. 14). They taunt him, Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come! (v. 15), though he has not run from being their shepherd and God knows what came out of his lips (v. 16). Be not a terror to me; you are my refuge in the day of disaster (v. 17), and he asks that his persecutors, not he, be put to shame (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who asked whether God was a failing brook now asks to be healed, and knows who alone can do it.

verseByVerse.quote: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise. Behold, they say to me, "Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come!" I have not run away from being your shepherd, nor have I desired the day of sickness. You know what came out of my lips; it was before your face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise.

The prophet prays, and the shape of the prayer is theology. Heal me... and I shall be healed. He does not say, help me to heal, or heal me so that I can recover. If God does it, it is done; if God does not, nothing else will.

This is the man who asked in chapter 8, Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? (8:22), and who accused God of being a brook that fails (15:18). Now he brings the wound to the only physician there is. Watch that progression in a person's life: from complaint about the absence of healing to a request for it.

Behold, they say to me, "Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come!"

The taunt of people who have heard the warnings for years and watched nothing happen. It is the mockery Peter predicted for the last days, asking where the promise of his coming is. Delay is read as disproof, and the challenge has a swagger to it: Let it come!

They got their wish within a few years.

I have not run away from being your shepherd, nor have I desired the day of sickness. You know what came out of my lips; it was before your face.

Two denials, and both matter. He has not deserted the flock, though everything in his circumstances invited it. And he has not desired the day of sickness — he has not wanted the disaster he preaches, which is the accusation people always make against the man who warns them.

His defence is simply that God heard him: You know what came out of my lips. A minister's real record is not the reputation he has among his hearers but what God heard him say.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not a terror to me; you are my refuge in the day of disaster. Let those be put to shame who persecute me, but let me not be put to shame; let them be dismayed, but let me not be dismayed; bring upon them the day of disaster; destroy them with double destruction!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not a terror to me; you are my refuge in the day of disaster.

A remarkable prayer, and an honest one. He asks God not to become the thing he is afraid of. When judgment is falling all around, the hand that sends it is the same hand he is sheltering under, and that is a hard place to stand.

Everyone who trusts God through a disaster knows this tension. The God who is my refuge is also the God who permitted the thing I need refuge from. Jeremiah does not resolve it; he prays it.

Let those be put to shame who persecute me, but let me not be put to shame; let them be dismayed, but let me not be dismayed; bring upon them the day of disaster; destroy them with double destruction!

The imprecation again, sharper than before. Read it as the prayer of a man who has been forbidden to defend himself and has handed the case over (11:20): everything he wants done to his enemies he asks God to do, which means he will do none of it himself.

Christians pray differently since Calvary, where the one who was persecuted asked for his enemies' forgiveness. But the instinct underneath — leave the judging to God, and say so out loud — is one the New Testament commends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — The Sabbath at the Gates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is sent to stand in the People's Gate and all the gates of Jerusalem (vv. 19-20): do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day, but keep the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers (vv. 21-22) — which their fathers refused to hear (v. 23). If they listen, kings and princes will enter these gates, the city will be inhabited forever, and worshippers will come from all Judah (vv. 24-26); if not, I will kindle a fire in its gates that will not be quenched (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole future of the city is hung on one visible, weekly act of trust.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus said the LORD to me: "Go and stand in the People's Gate, by which the kings of Judah enter and by which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem, and say: 'Hear the word of the LORD, you kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who enter by these gates. Thus says the LORD: Take care for the sake of your lives, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem. And do not carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath or do any work, but keep the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers. Yet they did not listen or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck, that they might not hear and receive instruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus said the LORD to me: "Go and stand in the People's Gate, by which the kings of Judah enter and by which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem, and say: 'Hear the word of the LORD, you kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who enter by these gates.

Another open-air sermon, and the location is chosen for traffic: the gate the royal household uses, and then every other gate in the city. Everyone entering will hear it.

Thus says the LORD: Take care for the sake of your lives, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem. And do not carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath or do any work, but keep the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers.

And the subject is the Sabbath. After chapters about idolatry, injustice, false prophets and a deceitful heart, God sends his prophet to talk about carrying loads on a Saturday.

It can look trivial until you see what the day was for. The Sabbath was the covenant sign worn in public, a weekly, visible statement that this people belonged to God, that their lives were not their own and that their provision did not depend on their own unbroken effort. A man who stops trading one day in seven is saying, out loud, that God feeds him. Bringing a burden in through the gate on that day was not a technicality; it was the trust of verse 7 denied in the street.

Isaiah put the invitation warmly: call the Sabbath a delight, and then you shall take delight in the LORD (Isa 58:13-14).

Yet they did not listen or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck, that they might not hear and receive instruction.

The verdict on the fathers, in the language of 7:26. Note the purpose clause: they stiffened their necks that they might not hear. The deafness was the objective, not the side effect.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But if you listen to me, declares the LORD, and bring in no burden by the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, but keep the Sabbath day holy and do no work on it, then there shall enter by the gates of this city kings and princes who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their officials, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And this city shall be inhabited forever. And people shall come from the cities of Judah and the places around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the Shephelah, from the hill country, and from the Negeb, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and bringing thank offerings to the house of the LORD. But if you do not listen to me, to keep the Sabbath day holy, and not to bear a burden and enter by the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, then I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem and shall not be quenched.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"'But if you listen to me, declares the LORD, and bring in no burden by the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, but keep the Sabbath day holy and do no work on it, then there shall enter by the gates of this city kings and princes who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their officials, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And this city shall be inhabited forever.

Now the two futures, and both of them run through the same gates.

If they listen: kings of David's line riding in, officials, crowds, and a city inhabited forever. The promise is enormous and it hangs on something small enough to see from the street. God often puts the weight of great things on one small, visible act of obedience, because that is where trust becomes concrete.

And people shall come from the cities of Judah and the places around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the Shephelah, from the hill country, and from the Negeb, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and bringing thank offerings to the house of the LORD.

Pilgrims from every region, with the whole range of offerings, and the list ends with thank offerings — the sacrifice that is not required by guilt but brought because someone is glad. That is the picture of a country put right with God: roads full of people who want to be there.

But if you do not listen to me, to keep the Sabbath day holy, and not to bear a burden and enter by the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, then I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem and shall not be quenched.'"

And the other future: fire in the gates, spreading to the palaces, unquenchable. That is exactly what happened in 587 BC.

For Christians the Sabbath command comes through Christ, who said The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and called himself lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28). Hebrews says that there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, entered by resting from our own works as God did from his (Heb 4:9-10).

So the question the chapter finally asks is the question of verses 5 and 7 in a practical form. Is your life arranged to say that God provides, or does it say that everything depends on your unbroken effort? The answer is visible in a diary, which is why God sent a prophet to stand at a gate and watch what people carried through it.

17.title: The Heart Is Deceitful: Two Trees and a Sabbath
17.overview:
Judah's sin is engraved with an iron pen on the tablet of their heart and on the horns of their altars, and their children remember the shrines; their treasures will become spoil and they will serve their enemies in an unknown land (vv. 1-4).

Two portraits follow. Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength: he is a shrub in a salt land who never sees good come (vv. 5-6). Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD: a tree planted by water, whose leaves stay green in the heat and who does not cease to bear fruit in the year of drought (vv. 7-8).

The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick, and no one can understand it — but God searches it and repays each according to his ways (vv. 9-10). Unjust riches leave a man like a partridge on another's eggs (v. 11). God's throne is the sanctuary, and those who forsake the fountain of living water are written in the earth (vv. 12-13). Jeremiah prays to be healed and saved, answers the taunt Where is the word of the LORD?, and asks God not to be a terror to him (vv. 14-18).

Finally he is sent to the gates to preach the Sabbath: if they keep it holy, kings will enter and the city will stand forever with pilgrims bringing thank offerings; if not, fire will devour the palaces (vv. 19-27).
17.theology:
Sin is engraved on the heart where God intends to write his law (v. 1; 31:33), and religion without repentance records guilt rather than removing it. Children learn what adults practise (v. 2).

Trust is the dividing line between two lives (vv. 5-8; Ps 1:1-3): misplaced trust is a heart turning away, and trust in God produces fruit precisely in the drought. The heart cannot be read by its owner (v. 9), only by God (v. 10; Ps 139:23-24), which is why it must be replaced, not reformed (31:33; Ezek 36:26).

God alone heals and saves (v. 14), and he may be both the one who sends disaster and the refuge in it (v. 17). The Sabbath was the visible weekly sign that life and provision come from God (vv. 21-27; Isa 58:13-14), fulfilled in Christ, lord of the Sabbath, and in the rest that remains for God's people (Mark 2:27-28; Heb 4:9-10).
17.examples:
An inscription cut with a diamond point, not a stain on the surface.

Sin carved into the horns of the altar, the furniture of forgiveness.

Grey scrub in a salt land: alive, and never flourishing.

Roots that reach water the drought cannot touch.

The instrument you would use to examine your heart is the heart.

A partridge brooding over eggs that run off to someone else.

A diary that says either God provides or everything depends on me.
