verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Down to the Potter's House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will let you hear my words (vv. 1-2). Jeremiah finds the potter working at his wheel (v. 3), and when the vessel was spoiled in the potter's hand he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do (v. 4). Then the word comes: can I not do with you as this potter has done?, for like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: God sends his prophet to a workshop to watch a craftsman start again with spoiled clay.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will let you hear my words." So I went down to the potter's house, and there he was working at his wheel. And the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will let you hear my words."

God's word does not always arrive in a temple or a vision. Here it is scheduled for a workshop in the lower city, and the prophet has to walk there to receive it. The ESV notes that the phrase may be rendered "will cause you to hear": the potter's shed is the appointed place of revelation.

Much of what God teaches is learned by watching ordinary work done well.

So I went down to the potter's house, and there he was working at his wheel.

The scene is domestic and unhurried: a man at a double wheel, kicking the lower stone, hands wet, shaping the clay on the upper one. Jeremiah stands and watches, and the sermon is the craftsman's hands.

And the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do.

Everything turns on this verse. The pot goes wrong — a stone in the clay, an uneven wall, a wobble — and the potter does not throw the lump away. He collapses it and starts again, making something else of it, as it seemed good to the potter to do.

Two things are true at once, and the chapter needs both. The potter has complete authority over the clay: the clay does not vote on what it becomes. And the potter does not discard spoiled clay: he reworks it. The God who is about to say terrifying things is first shown as a craftsman who will not bin the material.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? declares the LORD. Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to me: "O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? declares the LORD. Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.

The interpretation is given as a question, and it is a question about rights. Can I not do with you as this potter has done? Israel had been arguing for chapters that God could not really destroy the temple, could not hand over his own city, would not do this to his people. The potter's wheel answers all of it.

Scripture uses the image both ways. Isaiah turns it into prayer: we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand (Isa 64:8) — which is the comfortable direction. And he turns it into rebuke: Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, "He did not make me"? (Isa 29:16). Paul takes it up for the hardest question in Romans: Has the potter no right over the clay? (Rom 9:21).

The point is not that people are inert lumps with no responsibility — the next six verses make that impossible to conclude. It is that God is not accountable to the clay for what he does with it, and that his freedom is exercised by a craftsman who reworks rather than discards.

Paul adds the note that keeps the image from crushing anyone: we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Cor 4:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here is the rule behind every prophecy: if God announces uprooting and that nation... turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended (vv. 7-8); and if he announces building and it does evil, then I will relent of the good that I had intended (vv. 9-10). So: Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way (v. 11). And the answer comes back: That is in vain! We will follow our own plans (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Warnings are conditional by design; they are offered so that they need not be carried out.

verseByVerse.quote: If at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom, that I will pluck up and break down and destroy it, and if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it. And if at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom that I will build and plant it, and if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it. Now, therefore, say to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: 'Thus says the LORD, Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way, and amend your ways and your deeds.' "But they say, 'That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom, that I will pluck up and break down and destroy it, and if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it.

Here is one of the most important paragraphs in the prophetic books, because it tells you how to read every threat in them. The verbs are the ones from Jeremiah's call — pluck up, break down, destroy (1:10) — and they are now shown to be conditional.

A prophecy of judgment is not a weather forecast. It is an announcement made in order to be falsified. God says what he intends to do so that the people will turn and he will not have to do it.

Jonah is the case study. He preached forty days and Nineveh would be overthrown, with no conditions attached; the city repented; and God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it (Jonah 3:10). Jonah was furious precisely because he knew this principle in advance.

And if at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom that I will build and plant it, and if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it.

And the rule runs the other way too, which is less often quoted. A promise of blessing is not a charm that survives rebellion. Judah's whole delusion was that the promises to David and to Zion had made them permanently safe, whatever they did.

Nothing here makes God changeable. His character and his purposes do not move; that is exactly why his response to a nation moves when the nation moves. A father who treats a repentant child the same as a defiant one is not steadfast but indifferent.

Now, therefore, say to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: 'Thus says the LORD, Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way, and amend your ways and your deeds.'

Notice the verb: I am shaping disaster. The potter is at the wheel again, and what is taking form on it is judgment — announced while it is still soft, still on the wheel, still capable of being collapsed and remade. Ezekiel puts God's heart in it plainly: I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, so turn, and live (Ezek 18:32).

"But they say, 'That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.'

And the answer is the most chilling sentence in the chapter, because it is not a denial. They do not say the message is false. They say That is in vain! — hopeless, no use, too late — and then announce that they will do as they please anyway.

Despair and defiance have arrived at the same place, as they often do. A person who says "I could never change" and a person who says "I will not change" end up doing exactly the same thing on Monday morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Does the Snow of Lebanon Leave?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ask among the nations, Who has heard the like of this? (v. 13). Snow does not desert the crags, and mountain streams do not run dry (v. 14), But my people have forgotten me, stumbling off the ancient roads onto side tracks (v. 15), so their land becomes a horror, a thing to be hissed at forever (v. 16). Like the east wind I will scatter them before the enemy. I will show them my back, not my face (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the weather keeps faith better than this people; what nature does by nature they would not do by covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD: Ask among the nations, Who has heard the like of this? The virgin Israel has done a very horrible thing. Does the snow of Lebanon leave the crags of Sirion? Do the mountain waters run dry, the cold flowing streams? But my people have forgotten me; they make offerings to false gods; they made them stumble in their ways, in the ancient roads, and to walk into side roads, not the highway, making their land a horror, a thing to be hissed at forever. Everyone who passes by it is horrified and shakes his head. Like the east wind I will scatter them before the enemy. I will show them my back, not my face, in the day of their calamity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore thus says the LORD: Ask among the nations, Who has heard the like of this? The virgin Israel has done a very horrible thing.

God calls for a survey again, as in 2:10. Go and ask the pagans whether they have ever heard of a people abandoning its own God. The behaviour is not merely wrong; it is unprecedented.

Does the snow of Lebanon leave the crags of Sirion? Do the mountain waters run dry, the cold flowing streams?

Two questions from geography. The snow on Hermon does not decide one year to be somewhere else. The cold streams that come off those mountains do not quit. The ESV notes two difficulties in the Hebrew here, but the sense is plain: nature is reliable.

That is the comparison — and it is the same one as chapter 8, where migrating birds kept their calendar. Creation does by instinct what Israel would not do by covenant.

But my people have forgotten me; they make offerings to false gods; they made them stumble in their ways, in the ancient roads, and to walk into side roads, not the highway,

The road image returns from 6:16, where they were told to ask for the ancient paths. Here the false gods have tripped them off the highway onto side tracks. Nobody plans to end up lost; they take a turning that looked reasonable.

making their land a horror, a thing to be hissed at forever. Everyone who passes by it is horrified and shakes his head.

The nation that was meant to make God known to the world becomes a roadside curiosity — a ruin travellers point at. Israel's calling was to be a witness; she will be one either way.

Like the east wind I will scatter them before the enemy. I will show them my back, not my face, in the day of their calamity."

The east wind is the desert sirocco that strips a field. And the last clause reverses the priestly blessing, in which the LORD makes his face shine upon his people: I will show them my back, not my face. The worst part of the judgment is not the wind but the turned back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Let Us Strike Him with the Tongue
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah, they say, since priest, wise man and prophet will still be there without him: let us strike him with the tongue (v. 18). He appeals: Should good be repaid with evil?, recalling how he stood before you to speak good for them (vv. 19-20). Then a prayer that spares nothing: famine and sword for their children, widowhood for their wives, and Forgive not their iniquity (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The man forbidden to defend himself hands everything to God, including a rage he does not disguise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah, for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and let us not pay attention to any of his words." Hear me, O LORD, and listen to the voice of my adversaries. Should good be repaid with evil? Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they said, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah, for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and let us not pay attention to any of his words."

Listen to their reasoning, because it is the reasoning of respectable religion defending itself. We still have priests for the law, sages for counsel and prophets for the word — the three offices are intact. So this one man can be removed without loss. The institution will carry on.

It is the argument every establishment makes against the person who says the establishment has gone wrong.

And the weapon is chosen: let us strike him with the tongue. Not a knife, at this stage — rumour, insinuation, official statements, the slow discrediting of a man. The psalm knows the method: they whet their tongues like swords and shoot from ambush at the blameless (Ps 64:3-4). And of Jesus, after Lazarus, from that day on they made plans to put him to death (John 11:53).

Hear me, O LORD, and listen to the voice of my adversaries. Should good be repaid with evil? Yet they have dug a pit for my life.

He takes it to God and asks him to listen to both sides: hear me, and hear them. The question that follows is the ache of the whole chapter: Should good be repaid with evil?

Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them.

And here is what makes their plot so bitter. All those forbidden prayers (7:16; 11:14; 14:11) were prayers for them. The man they are trying to kill is the man who has been standing between them and God's wrath. They never knew it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore deliver up their children to famine; give them over to the power of the sword; let their wives become childless and widowed. May their men meet death by pestilence, their youths be struck down by the sword in battle. May a cry be heard from their houses, when you bring the plunderer suddenly upon them! For they have dug a pit to take me and laid snares for my feet. Yet you, O LORD, know all their plotting to kill me. Forgive not their iniquity, nor blot out their sin from your sight. Let them be overthrown before you; deal with them in the time of your anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore deliver up their children to famine; give them over to the power of the sword; let their wives become childless and widowed. May their men meet death by pestilence, their youths be struck down by the sword in battle.

This is the hardest passage in the book to read as a Christian, and it should not be softened. Jeremiah asks God to bring famine on their children and widowhood on their wives.

Several things need saying, and none of them is that the prayer is model devotion.

First, it is a prayer and not a plan. Everything he wants done he asks God to do; he lifts no hand himself, and he goes on living among these people. The alternative to praying rage is usually acting it.

Second, what he asks for is exactly the judgment God has already announced on the nation (14:12, 16). He is not inventing a punishment; he is asking God to do what he has said, and to do it now, because these men are murdering the messenger.

Third, Scripture records it without approving it. The Bible is an honest book about its heroes, and this is a man at the end of his strength who has been threatened by his own village, plotted against by the clergy, and forbidden to defend himself.

May a cry be heard from their houses, when you bring the plunderer suddenly upon them! For they have dug a pit to take me and laid snares for my feet. Yet you, O LORD, know all their plotting to kill me. Forgive not their iniquity, nor blot out their sin from your sight. Let them be overthrown before you; deal with them in the time of your anger.

Forgive not their iniquity is the line no Christian can pray, and the reason is not that we are nicer than Jeremiah. It is that we stand on the other side of a cross where the one plotted against said, Father, forgive them, they know not what they do — the prayer this chapter could not reach.

And yet the instinct underneath is one the New Testament keeps: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God. Jeremiah's fury is handed over. That is not the last word on prayer, and it is a great deal better than the pit he was heading for.

What this passage gives a suffering believer is permission to be honest. God can be told the truth about what you feel toward people who have wrecked your life, and the telling is safer than the silence.

18.title: The Potter and the Clay
18.overview:
God sends Jeremiah to a potter's workshop. The vessel is spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworks it into another as it seems good to him (vv. 1-4). So, God says, is Israel in his hand (vv. 5-6).

Then the rule that governs prophecy: if God announces disaster on a nation and it turns from its evil, he will relent; if he promises good and it does evil, he will relent of the good (vv. 7-10). Therefore he is shaping disaster against Judah and calling them to return (v. 11) — and they answer, That is in vain! We will follow our own plans (v. 12).

No nation has heard the like: snow does not leave the mountains and streams do not run dry, but God's people have forgotten him and been tripped off the ancient roads, so their land will be a horror and he will show them his back and not his face (vv. 13-17). The men of Judah plot to strike him with the tongue, reasoning that priest, sage and prophet remain without him (v. 18). Jeremiah asks whether good should be repaid with evil, recalls that he stood before God to speak good for them, and pours out a prayer for their destruction (vv. 19-23).
18.theology:
God has absolute right over his people as a potter over clay (vv. 5-6; Isa 29:16; Rom 9:21), and he is a potter who reworks spoiled clay rather than discarding it (v. 4; Isa 64:8).

Prophecies of judgment and promises of blessing are conditional by design (vv. 7-10): warnings are given so that they need not be fulfilled (Jonah 3:10; Ezek 18:30-32), and promises do not shelter the unrepentant. God's consistency is the reason his response changes when people change.

Despair (That is in vain!) and defiance end in the same conduct (v. 12). Opposition to God's word often comes from intact religious institutions defending themselves (v. 18). The imprecation of vv. 21-23 hands rage to God rather than acting on it, and stands this side of Luke 23:34 as something Scripture records rather than commends.
18.examples:
A craftsman collapsing a spoiled pot and starting again with the same clay.

A warning issued in the hope of being proved wrong.

"I could never change" and "I will not change" doing the same thing on Monday.

Snow that never decides to be somewhere else.

Striking a man with the tongue rather than the knife.

The man they plotted to kill was the one praying for them.

19.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD, "Go, buy a potter's earthenware flask, and take some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests,<sup>2</sup>and go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the entry of the Potsherd Gate, and proclaim there the words that I tell you.<sup>3</sup>You shall say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing such disaster upon this place that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle.<sup>4</sup>Because the people have forsaken me and have profaned this place by making offerings in it to other gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known; and because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents,<sup>5</sup>and have built the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire as burnt offerings to Baal, which I did not command or decree, nor did it come into my mind—<sup>6</sup>therefore, behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.<sup>7</sup>And in this place I will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem, and will cause their people to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hand of those who seek their life. I will give their dead bodies for food to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth.<sup>8</sup>And I will make this city a horror, a thing to be hissed at. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds.<sup>9</sup>And I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and their daughters, and everyone shall eat the flesh of his neighbor in the siege and in the distress, with which their enemies and those who seek their life afflict them.'<sup>10</sup>"Then you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you,<sup>11</sup>and shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended. Men shall bury in Topheth because there will be no place else to bury.<sup>12</sup>Thus will I do to this place, declares the LORD, and to its inhabitants, making this city like Topheth.<sup>13</sup>The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah— all the houses on whose roofs offerings have been offered to all the host of heaven, and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods—shall be defiled like the place of Topheth.'"<sup>14</sup>Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD's house and said to all the people:<sup>15</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the disaster that I have pronounced against it, because they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Go to the Valley and Take Witnesses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Go, buy a potter's earthenware flask, and take elders of the people and of the priests (v. 1), out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the entry of the Potsherd Gate (v. 2). There he announces disaster so great that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle (v. 3), because they have forsaken God, profaned the place, filled it with the blood of innocents (v. 4) and burned their sons to Baal — which I did not command or decree, nor did it come into my mind (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The sermon is preached at the scene of the crime, with the establishment brought along as witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, "Go, buy a potter's earthenware flask, and take some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests, and go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the entry of the Potsherd Gate, and proclaim there the words that I tell you. You shall say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing such disaster upon this place that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle. Because the people have forsaken me and have profaned this place by making offerings in it to other gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known; and because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents, and have built the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire as burnt offerings to Baal, which I did not command or decree, nor did it come into my mind—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD, "Go, buy a potter's earthenware flask, and take some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests,

Chapter 18 was clay on a wheel, soft and workable. Chapter 19 is a finished flask, fired hard in a kiln. The material has changed, and so has the message.

And this time there is an audience of dignitaries. He is to bring elders of the people and elders of the priests — civic and religious leadership together, the men whose testimony cannot later be dismissed. Whatever happens, there will be witnesses.

and go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the entry of the Potsherd Gate, and proclaim there the words that I tell you.

The location is chosen with terrible precision. The Valley of Hinnom is where children were burned (7:31). The Potsherd Gate is, by its name, where the city's broken pottery went out — the rubbish tip. A sermon about a smashed jar, preached at the gate where smashed jars are thrown, in the valley where they burned their children.

You shall say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing such disaster upon this place that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle.

The ears... will tingle is the phrase used when Samuel was told of the fall of Eli's house, and when Kings describes the end of Jerusalem. It means news so shocking that people flinch when they hear it.

Because the people have forsaken me and have profaned this place by making offerings in it to other gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known; and because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents, and have built the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire as burnt offerings to Baal, which I did not command or decree, nor did it come into my mind—

The indictment has three counts: forsaking God, profaning the place, and the blood of innocents. And then the specific horror, child sacrifice, with the same phrase as the temple sermon: nor did it come into my mind.

God's repeated insistence on this matters. A religion that burns children cannot claim any connection to him. When people do appalling things in God's name, the question to ask is whether he ever said it — and Scripture, not sincerity, is where that is settled.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter (v. 6). There God will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem and give their bodies to the birds (v. 7); the city will be a horror, a thing to be hissed at (v. 8); and in the siege they will eat the flesh of their own children and of one another (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where children were burned is renamed for what will be done in it.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore, behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. And in this place I will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem, and will cause their people to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hand of those who seek their life. I will give their dead bodies for food to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth. And I will make this city a horror, a thing to be hissed at. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds. And I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and their daughters, and everyone shall eat the flesh of his neighbor in the siege and in the distress, with which their enemies and those who seek their life afflict them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
therefore, behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.

The renaming of 7:32 is repeated on the spot. God changes the name of the place to describe what will happen there. Judgment is fitted to the crime so exactly that the map itself records it.

And in this place I will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem, and will cause their people to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hand of those who seek their life. I will give their dead bodies for food to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth.

I will make void the plans — literally empty them out, as one empties a jar. The word suits the prop in his hand. All the policy, the alliances with Egypt, the calculations of the court: poured out on the ground.

And I will make this city a horror, a thing to be hissed at. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds.

The city that was to be a light draws the sharp intake of breath that travellers give at a ruin.

And I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and their daughters, and everyone shall eat the flesh of his neighbor in the siege and in the distress, with which their enemies and those who seek their life afflict them.'

This is unbearable to read, and it happened. Lamentations, written by the same man after the siege, records that compassionate women boiled their own children.

Note the dreadful symmetry. They gave their children to the fire in this valley as an act of religion; in the siege they will eat them to stay alive. Sin's logic works itself out to the end, and the end is always worse than the beginning promised.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — So Will I Break This People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you (v. 10), and say: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended, with burials in Topheth for want of room (v. 11). The city will be made like Topheth (v. 12), and every house whose roof has carried offerings to the host of heaven will be defiled (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Yesterday's clay could be reworked; a fired flask smashed on the rocks cannot, and that is the point.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you, and shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended. Men shall bury in Topheth because there will be no place else to bury. Thus will I do to this place, declares the LORD, and to its inhabitants, making this city like Topheth. The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah— all the houses on whose roofs offerings have been offered to all the host of heaven, and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods—shall be defiled like the place of Topheth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you,

The sermon becomes an action. He has carried the jar all the way out to the valley; now, in front of the elders, he throws it down.

and shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended.

And here is why the flask is fired and not wet. Soft clay can be collapsed and reworked (18:4); a kiln-hardened pot smashed on stones is finished. So that it can never be mended.

Put the two chapters together and you have the whole message. While the clay is soft, God says: return, and I will rework you. When it has been fired hard by years of refusal, there comes a moment when the pot is thrown down. The difference between the chapters is not a change in God but a change in what the clay has become.

Scripture keeps this image for royal judgment too: You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel (Ps 2:9), applied to the risen Christ in Revelation (Rev 2:27). And Lamentations mourns that the precious sons of Zion are regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter's hands (Lam 4:2).

Men shall bury in Topheth because there will be no place else to bury. Thus will I do to this place, declares the LORD, and to its inhabitants, making this city like Topheth.

The whole city will become what this valley was: a place of the dead. The rubbish tip spreads until it is the capital.

The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah— all the houses on whose roofs offerings have been offered to all the host of heaven, and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods—shall be defiled like the place of Topheth.'"

Flat roofs were where families slept in summer and where, it turns out, they had been burning incense to the stars. Household religion, conducted upstairs, in private, by respectable people. Those houses will be as unclean as the valley of burning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — From Topheth to the Temple Court
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD's house (v. 14) and said to all the people that God is bringing on the city all the disaster he has pronounced, because they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: He carries the broken-flask message straight from the rubbish valley into the temple courtyard, and it costs him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD's house and said to all the people: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the disaster that I have pronounced against it, because they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD's house and said to all the people:

He walks up out of the valley and straight into the temple courtyard, with the dust of the broken flask still on him, and preaches it again to the crowd. Nothing is toned down for the religious venue.

This is the same courtyard as the temple sermon of chapter 7. He knows exactly what it costs to say these things here, and the first two verses of the next chapter record the result: the chief officer of the temple has him beaten and put in the stocks overnight.

"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the disaster that I have pronounced against it, because they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words."

The summary is short and the reason is one clause: they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words. Not their idolatry, not the blood, not the injustice — behind all of them, the refusal to listen.

That is the thread from chapter 7 to here, and it is the thread a reader should follow home. Everything in Jeremiah begins with hearing. The people who would not hear became people who could not (6:10), and the flask was fired hard in exactly that oven.

19.title: The Broken Flask
19.overview:
God tells Jeremiah to buy a fired clay flask and take elders of the people and the priests out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the Potsherd Gate (vv. 1-2). There he announces disaster that will make ears tingle, because they have forsaken God, profaned the place, filled it with innocent blood and burned their sons to Baal — something that never came into God's mind (vv. 3-5).

The valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter; God will empty out the plans of Judah, give their bodies to the birds, make the city a horror, and reduce them in the siege to eating their own children (vv. 6-9).

Then Jeremiah breaks the flask in front of the witnesses: so God will break this people and this city, so that it can never be mended, until Topheth becomes a graveyard and every roof where incense was burned to the stars is defiled (vv. 10-13). He returns from Topheth to the temple court and repeats the message to everyone, because they have stiffened their neck and refused to hear (vv. 14-15).
19.theology:
God distances himself absolutely from atrocity done in his name: child sacrifice never came into his mind (v. 5; 7:31). Judgment is fitted to the sin, to the point of renaming the place where it happened (v. 6).

The soft clay of ch. 18 could be reworked; the fired flask of ch. 19 is broken beyond mending (vv. 10-11). The difference lies not in God but in what long refusal has made of the people (6:10). Compare Ps 2:9 and Rev 2:27, where the same image belongs to the reign of Christ.

Private household religion is not hidden from God (v. 13), and the root of every charge in the chapter is the refusal to hear his words (v. 15).
19.examples:
A sermon about a smashed jar, preached at the gate where the city threw its broken pots.

Bringing the elders along so nobody can say later that it was not said.

Plans emptied out on the ground like water from a jar.

Soft clay reworked; fired clay thrown down.

Incense to the stars, burned on the roof by respectable families.

Walking from the rubbish valley into the temple courtyard without softening a word.

20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Pashhur the priest, the son of Immer, who was chief officer in the house of the LORD, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things.<sup>2</sup>Then Pashhur beat Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper Benjamin Gate of the house of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>The next day, when Pashhur released Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah said to him, "The LORD does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side.<sup>4</sup>For thus says the LORD: Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They shall fall by the sword of their enemies while you look on. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon. He shall carry them captive to Babylon, and shall strike them down with the sword.<sup>5</sup>Moreover, I will give all the wealth of the city, all its gains, all its prized belongings, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah into the hand of their enemies, who shall plunder them and seize them and carry them to Babylon.<sup>6</sup>And you, Pashhur, and all who dwell in your house, shall go into captivity. To Babylon you shall go, and there you shall die, and there you shall be buried, you and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely."<sup>7</sup>O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed. I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me.<sup>8</sup>For whenever I speak, I cry out, I shout, "Violence and destruction!" For the word of the LORD has become for me a reproach and derision all day long.<sup>9</sup>If I say, "I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name," there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.<sup>10</sup>For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! "Denounce him! Let us denounce him!" say all my close friends, watching for my fall. "Perhaps he will be deceived; then we can overcome him and take our revenge on him."<sup>11</sup>But the LORD is with me as a dread warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble; they will not overcome me. They will be greatly shamed, for they will not succeed. Their eternal dishonor will never be forgotten.<sup>12</sup>O LORD of hosts, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause.<sup>13</sup>Sing to the LORD; praise the LORD! For he has delivered the life of the needy from the hand of evildoers.<sup>14</sup>Cursed be the day on which I was born! The day when my mother bore me, let it not be blessed!<sup>15</sup>Cursed be the man who brought the news to my father, "A son is born to you," making him very glad.<sup>16</sup>Let that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without pity; let him hear a cry in the morning and an alarm at noon,<sup>17</sup>because he did not kill me in the womb; so my mother would have been my grave, and her womb forever great.<sup>18</sup>Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Beaten and Put in the Stocks
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pashhur, chief officer in the house of the LORD, hears Jeremiah and has him beaten and locked in the stocks at the upper Benjamin Gate (vv. 1-2). Released next morning, Jeremiah renames him: The LORD does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side (v. 3). He will be a terror to himself and his friends, watching them fall (v. 4); the city's wealth will go to Babylon (v. 5); and Pashhur will die in exile, you and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The first physical violence against Jeremiah is ordered by the man in charge of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Pashhur the priest, the son of Immer, who was chief officer in the house of the LORD, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things. Then Pashhur beat Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper Benjamin Gate of the house of the LORD. The next day, when Pashhur released Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah said to him, "The LORD does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Pashhur the priest, the son of Immer, who was chief officer in the house of the LORD, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things. Then Pashhur beat Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper Benjamin Gate of the house of the LORD.

Chapter 19 ended with Jeremiah preaching in the temple court. This is what happened next, and it is the first recorded violence against him.

Note who does it. Not a mob, not the Babylonians, not the palace: the priest, chief officer in the house of the LORD, the man responsible for order in the temple. He has the prophet flogged — forty lashes less one was the legal limit — and clamped overnight in stocks that twisted the body into a fixed, painful position, in a public gateway where everyone going in to worship could see him.

Religious institutions can be the most efficient persecutors, because they have authority, premises and the confidence of being on God's side. The apostles were flogged by the council for preaching and left rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name (Acts 5:41). Paul took the thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Cor 11:24). Hebrews sums up the line Jeremiah stands in: Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment, of whom the world was not worthy (Heb 11:36, 38).

The next day, when Pashhur released Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah said to him, "The LORD does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side.

He comes out of the stocks stiff, bleeding and still preaching. His first act is to rename his jailer.

Terror on Every Side is the phrase that has been running through the book for the siege (6:25), and in a few verses it will be what his enemies whisper about him (20:10). Pashhur will not merely witness the terror; he will be it, to himself and to everyone near him.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They shall fall by the sword of their enemies while you look on. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon. He shall carry them captive to Babylon, and shall strike them down with the sword. Moreover, I will give all the wealth of the city, all its gains, all its prized belongings, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah into the hand of their enemies, who shall plunder them and seize them and carry them to Babylon. And you, Pashhur, and all who dwell in your house, shall go into captivity. To Babylon you shall go, and there you shall die, and there you shall be buried, you and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD: Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They shall fall by the sword of their enemies while you look on. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon. He shall carry them captive to Babylon, and shall strike them down with the sword.

A terror to yourself is a terrible sentence. The man who inflicted fear will become the thing he cannot escape, because it is inside him. And he will watch his friends die: not spared, not blinded, but made to look on.

Moreover, I will give all the wealth of the city, all its gains, all its prized belongings, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah into the hand of their enemies, who shall plunder them and seize them and carry them to Babylon.

Four words for what the city owned — wealth, gains, prized belongings, treasures — and one verb for what happens to all of it. The temple treasury that Pashhur administered is included.

And you, Pashhur, and all who dwell in your house, shall go into captivity. To Babylon you shall go, and there you shall die, and there you shall be buried, you and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely."

The sentence is personal and specific: you will go, you will die there, you will be buried there. For a man whose identity was bound up with the temple in Jerusalem, dying in Babylon is the complete undoing of his life.

And the last clause names the real crime. Not the beating: you have prophesied falsely. Pashhur had been telling people what they wanted to hear, and the men who believed him will die in exile beside him. Comfortable preaching has casualties, and they include the preacher.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — A Fire Shut Up in My Bones
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed (v. 7): the word has made him a reproach and derision all day long (v. 8). Yet when he resolves to stop, it is as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot (v. 9). Friends watch for his fall (v. 10), But the LORD is with me as a dread warrior (v. 11); he commits his cause to the God who sees the heart and the mind (v. 12) and breaks into praise (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Complaint, compulsion, confidence and praise in seven verses, all of them honest at once.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed. I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me. For whenever I speak, I cry out, I shout, "Violence and destruction!" For the word of the LORD has become for me a reproach and derision all day long. If I say, "I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name," there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed. I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me.

Straight from the stocks to the sharpest words anyone in Scripture addresses to God. You have deceived me. The verb is strong; it is used of persuading someone into something they would not otherwise have chosen, and of seduction.

What does he mean? Not that God lied. He means that when he was called he did not know what it would cost, that God overpowered his objections (you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed), and that the life he was drawn into has made him the joke of the city. Every day. From everyone.

The Bible prints this. That is the first thing to notice. There is no editorial note correcting him, no lightning bolt, no rebuke in the next verse. God can be spoken to like this by a man at the end of his endurance, and the words are preserved in holy Scripture for every believer who has felt them and been afraid to say them.

For whenever I speak, I cry out, I shout, "Violence and destruction!" For the word of the LORD has become for me a reproach and derision all day long.

He cannot open his mouth without announcing catastrophe, and it has made him ridiculous. The word that was a joy and the delight of my heart (15:16) is now a reproach and derision. Both are true of the same word in the same man's life.

If I say, "I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name," there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.

So he tries the obvious solution: resign. Stop saying the name. And he finds he cannot, because the word he has swallowed burns. God had told him at the start that his words would be a fire in the prophet's mouth (5:14), and later asks, is not my word like fire (23:29).

This is one of the most exact descriptions of a calling ever written. He is not continuing because he feels strong, or because it is going well, or because anyone thanks him. He continues because stopping is worse. Anyone who has ever said, I cannot keep doing this — and has kept doing it — knows the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! "Denounce him! Let us denounce him!" say all my close friends, watching for my fall. "Perhaps he will be deceived; then we can overcome him and take our revenge on him." But the LORD is with me as a dread warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble; they will not overcome me. They will be greatly shamed, for they will not succeed. Their eternal dishonor will never be forgotten. O LORD of hosts, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause. Sing to the LORD; praise the LORD! For he has delivered the life of the needy from the hand of evildoers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! "Denounce him! Let us denounce him!" say all my close friends, watching for my fall. "Perhaps he will be deceived; then we can overcome him and take our revenge on him."

The phrase he gave Pashhur comes back at him: Terror is on every side! They have turned his own preaching into a nickname for him.

And the worst detail is all my close friends, watching for my fall. Not enemies — the men he ate with, hoping he will slip so they can be rid of him. The psalms know this pain, and so did Jesus at a table with the twelve.

But the LORD is with me as a dread warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble; they will not overcome me. They will be greatly shamed, for they will not succeed. Their eternal dishonor will never be forgotten.

And then, without transition, faith. The LORD is with me as a dread warrior — the promise of 1:8 and 1:19 held onto in the dark, and pictured as a champion standing at his shoulder.

Notice that nothing in his circumstances has changed between verse 10 and verse 11. The whispering continues. What has changed is what he is looking at.

O LORD of hosts, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause.

The words of 11:20 again, and the ESV notes that mind is in Hebrew "kidneys" — the innermost self. The last clause is the discipline of his whole life: to you have I committed my cause. He hands the file over.

Sing to the LORD; praise the LORD! For he has delivered the life of the needy from the hand of evildoers.

And he sings. In the space of seven verses: you deceived me, I cannot stop, they are all against me, God is with me, sing to the LORD. That is not inconsistency; it is what a real prayer life looks like from inside a real crisis.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cursed be the day on which I was born! (v. 14), and cursed the man who carried the good news to his father (v. 15), who should have killed him in the womb (vv. 16-17). Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame? (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The praise of verse 13 is followed immediately by the darkest words he ever speaks, and Scripture keeps both.

verseByVerse.quote: Cursed be the day on which I was born! The day when my mother bore me, let it not be blessed! Cursed be the man who brought the news to my father, "A son is born to you," making him very glad. Let that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without pity; let him hear a cry in the morning and an alarm at noon, because he did not kill me in the womb; so my mother would have been my grave, and her womb forever great. Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cursed be the day on which I was born! The day when my mother bore me, let it not be blessed!

And then, immediately after the praise, the darkest words in the book. The order matters: verse 13 sings, verse 14 curses. Whoever assembled this chapter did not tidy it.

He does not curse God, and he does not curse his mother. He curses a day — a thing that cannot be harmed by it. It is the cry of someone who wants the fact of his own existence undone. Job did the same in the ashes: Let the day perish on which I was born (Job 3:3).

Cursed be the man who brought the news to my father, "A son is born to you," making him very glad. Let that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without pity; let him hear a cry in the morning and an alarm at noon,

The messenger who ran to tell his father the happy news, who did nothing but carry good tidings, is cursed too. That is how far the grief reaches: back to the moment of gladness at his birth.

because he did not kill me in the womb; so my mother would have been my grave, and her womb forever great. Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame?

The chapter ends there. No answer, no divine reply, no resolution. Just the question: Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow?

Several things should be said, gently.

This is despair, and Scripture neither commends it nor condemns it here; it records it. A man called before birth (1:5) now wishes that birth had never happened — and the book that contains this also contains 1:5. Both belong to the same life.

If you have ever felt this, you are not outside the company of God's servants. Job said it, and Jeremiah, and neither was cast off. What God does with such words is keep them, and keep the man.

And there is one more thing. There was a greater prophet who was also mocked all the day — All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me (Ps 22:7) — whose close friends betrayed him, who sweated like blood and asked for the cup to pass (Luke 22:44). He did not curse the day he was born. He was born for that day, and went through it, so that people who curse their own birthdays might be born again.

20.title: Terror on Every Side: The Prophet in the Stocks
20.overview:
Pashhur, the chief officer of the temple, hears Jeremiah, has him beaten and locks him overnight in the stocks at the Benjamin Gate (vv. 1-2). Released, Jeremiah renames him Terror on Every Side and announces that he will be a terror to himself and his friends, that the city's wealth will go to Babylon, and that he will die and be buried there with all those to whom he prophesied falsely (vv. 3-6).

Then the last and sharpest of the confessions. O LORD, you have deceived me: the word has made him a laughingstock, yet when he resolves to stop it becomes a fire shut up in his bones that he cannot hold in (vv. 7-9). His close friends watch for his fall (v. 10), but the LORD is with him as a dread warrior; he commits his cause to God and calls for praise (vv. 11-13).

And immediately he curses the day of his birth and the man who announced it, wishing the womb had been his grave, and ends asking why he was born to see toil and sorrow (vv. 14-18).
20.theology:
Persecution of God's messengers often comes from religious authority (vv. 1-2; Acts 5:40-41). False preaching destroys the preacher and those who believed him (v. 6).

Scripture preserves a servant's accusation that God deceived and overpowered him (v. 7) without rebuke, showing that God can bear honest speech from exhausted people. A true calling continues not by enthusiasm but by compulsion: the word burns if withheld (v. 9; 23:29).

Faith and despair can occupy the same page: praise in v. 13 and a cursed birthday in v. 14. God keeps both, and keeps the man (compare 1:5). Christ, mocked all day and betrayed by his friends (Ps 22:6-8; Luke 22:44), was born for the day Jeremiah wished away.
20.examples:
The man in charge of the temple ordering the flogging.

Coming out of the stocks stiff and bleeding, and preaching first.

Resigning, and discovering you cannot.

Close friends waiting for you to slip.

Praise in one verse and a cursed birthday in the next, with nothing tidied away.
