Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds and will make him withdraw from us."<sup>3</sup>Then Jeremiah said to them: "Thus you shall say to Zedekiah,<sup>4</sup>'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands and with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and against the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the walls. And I will bring them together into the midst of this city.<sup>5</sup>I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath.<sup>6</sup>And I will strike down the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast. They shall die of a great pestilence.<sup>7</sup>Afterward, declares the LORD, I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his servants and the people in this city who survive the pestilence, sword, and famine into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of their enemies, into the hand of those who seek their lives. He shall strike them down with the edge of the sword. He shall not pity them or spare them or have compassion.'<sup>8</sup>"And to this people you shall say: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.<sup>9</sup>He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you shall live and shall have his life as a prize of war.<sup>10</sup>For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good, declares the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.'<sup>11</sup>"And to the house of the king of Judah say, 'Hear the word of the LORD,<sup>12</sup>O house of David! Thus says the LORD: "'Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of your evil deeds.'"<sup>13</sup>"Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain, declares the LORD; you who say, 'Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations?'<sup>14</sup>I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares the LORD; I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Myself Will Fight Against You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah sends Pashhur and Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to Inquire of the LORD for us, since Nebuchadnezzar is making war, hoping God will make him withdraw from us (vv. 1-2). The answer is the opposite of what they want: God will turn their own weapons back on them and gather the enemy inside the city (vv. 3-4). I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath (v. 5); man and beast will die of pestilence (v. 6), and the survivors, with Zedekiah, will be handed to Babylon, which shall not pity them or spare them or have compassion (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A king asks for a miracle like the old days and is told that the God of the exodus is now on the other side.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchiah and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, saying, "Inquire of the LORD for us, for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is making war against us. Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds and will make him withdraw from us." Then Jeremiah said to them: "Thus you shall say to Zedekiah, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands and with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and against the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the walls. And I will bring them together into the midst of this city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchiah and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, saying,

The book jumps forward about twenty years. Josiah is long dead, Jehoiakim too; Zedekiah is the last king of Judah, and Nebuchadnezzar's army is outside the walls. This Pashhur is a different man from the priest who flogged Jeremiah in chapter 20.

Notice the irony. For decades the palace has ignored, imprisoned and beaten this man. Now that the siege lines are up, the king sends an official delegation to ask him to pray.

"Inquire of the LORD for us, for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is making war against us. Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds and will make him withdraw from us."

The request is entirely religious and entirely hollow. Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds — they are thinking of the night the Assyrian army melted away outside these same walls in Hezekiah's day. Do that again.

The ESV notes that from this chapter on the Hebrew spells the king's name Nebuchadrezzar, and that the ESV uses the familiar form throughout.

What is missing from the request is any mention of repentance. They want the outcome Hezekiah got without the posture Hezekiah had. Prayer as a last-resort lever, offered by men who have not changed their minds about anything, is exactly what chapter 14 refused.

Then Jeremiah said to them: "Thus you shall say to Zedekiah, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands and with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and against the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the walls. And I will bring them together into the midst of this city.

The answer is not merely no. God says he will turn back the weapons in their hands — the defence itself will fail inward, and the fighting will end up in the streets rather than at the walls.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath. And I will strike down the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast. They shall die of a great pestilence. Afterward, declares the LORD, I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his servants and the people in this city who survive the pestilence, sword, and famine into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of their enemies, into the hand of those who seek their lives. He shall strike them down with the edge of the sword. He shall not pity them or spare them or have compassion.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath.

This is the most shocking sentence in the chapter, and it is shocking because of where the words come from. Outstretched hand and strong arm is exodus language: it is how Israel described God's rescue from Egypt, recited at every Passover.

Now the arm is stretched out against them. The God who fought for them fights against them, with three words for his wrath piled up. Zedekiah asked for a repeat of the old wonders; he is told the old wonders are being reversed.

There is no more sobering possibility in Scripture than this: to be on the wrong side of the God you claim as yours.

And I will strike down the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast. They shall die of a great pestilence.

Disease in a besieged city, with the water fouled and the dead unburied, needs no explanation. It killed more than the swords did.

Afterward, declares the LORD, I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his servants and the people in this city who survive the pestilence, sword, and famine into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of their enemies, into the hand of those who seek their lives. He shall strike them down with the edge of the sword. He shall not pity them or spare them or have compassion.'

The king is named, and his fate is spelled out to his own messengers. The three verbs of withheld mercy — no pity, no sparing, no compassion — were used of God in 13:14; here they describe the man he is handing them to. Babylon will not be gentle, and God says so in advance rather than letting them imagine a negotiated peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — Life and Death Set Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To the people: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death (v. 8). Staying in the city means sword, famine and pestilence; surrendering to the Chaldeans means life, and shall have his life as a prize of war (v. 9). For God has set my face against this city for harm and not for good, and it will be burned (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The way of life runs out through the gate of surrender, which is why the offer sounds like treason.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to this people you shall say: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you shall live and shall have his life as a prize of war. For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good, declares the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And to this people you shall say: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.

The words are Moses' words. At the end of Deuteronomy he set the same choice before the nation: I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life (Deut 30:19). Jesus put it as two gates and two roads, one wide and easy, one narrow and hard (Matt 7:13-14).

What is startling here is the content of the two ways.

He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you shall live and shall have his life as a prize of war.

The way of life is surrender. Walk out of the gate, hands empty, and give yourself up to the enemy — and you will keep your life, though nothing else, as a prize of war, the way a soldier keeps his skin when everything else is lost.

No wonder they called Jeremiah a traitor. This is the sermon that later gets him thrown into a cistern for demoralising the troops (38:4). He is telling a besieged city to give in, and he is telling them so because the siege is God's judgment and resisting it is resisting God.

There is a hard and useful lesson in it. Sometimes the godly response to a disaster we have brought on ourselves is not to fight for the position we held but to surrender it and accept the loss, because the discipline is from God and the life on the other side of it is real. Surrender looks like defeat and is the only way out.

For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good, declares the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.'

The city itself is not being saved. Individuals within it still can be, one at a time, by walking out. Judgment on a community and mercy to persons inside it are not contradictory, and this verse holds them together.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Execute Justice in the Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To the royal house: Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, or God's wrath will burn unquenched (vv. 11-12). Against the city trusting its position — Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations? (v. 13) — God says, I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, kindling a fire that devours everything round about (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Even at this hour the word to the palace is not military but moral: do justice before breakfast.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the house of the king of Judah say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O house of David! Thus says the LORD: "'Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of your evil deeds.'" "Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain, declares the LORD; you who say, 'Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations?' I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares the LORD; I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And to the house of the king of Judah say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O house of David! Thus says the LORD: "'Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of your evil deeds.'"

With an army at the gates, the word to the royal household is about the courts. Execute justice in the morning — the king's bench sat early, and the phrase means: make this the first business of the day, before anything else.

And the concrete duty is named: deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. Not issue a statement about justice; get the stolen thing back to the person it was taken from.

This is the measure by which the house of David is judged all through the prophets. Not the size of the army or the splendour of the temple, but whether a poor man who has been cheated can get a hearing before lunch.

"Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain, declares the LORD; you who say, 'Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations?'

Jerusalem sits on rock above its valleys, and the confidence in that geography has become a slogan: Who shall come down against us? Good walls in a good position, and the question is asked as if it had no answer.

God's reply is the opening words: I am against you. That is the answer to the question. It is not the Babylonians coming down; it is God.

I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares the LORD; I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her."

According to the fruit of your deeds — the harvest language of 17:10, where God searches the heart and gives each according to his ways. The fire kindled in the forest is probably the cedar palaces of the royal quarter, which the next chapter addresses directly.

The chapter that began with a king asking for a miracle ends with God pointing at the palace and telling him where the fire will start.

21.title: The Way of Life and the Way of Death
21.overview:
With Nebuchadnezzar's army at the walls, King Zedekiah sends officials to ask Jeremiah to enquire of the LORD, hoping for a repeat of God's past wonders (vv. 1-2). The answer is that God will turn their own weapons back on them and gather the enemy inside the city (vv. 3-4); he himself will fight against them with the outstretched arm of the exodus, in anger and fury; pestilence will kill man and beast; and Zedekiah and the survivors will be handed to a king who will not pity or spare them (vv. 5-7).

To the people God sets the way of life and the way of death: staying in the city means sword, famine and pestilence, while surrendering to the Chaldeans means keeping one's life as a prize of war, for God has set his face against the city and it will be burned (vv. 8-10).

To the house of David the word is to execute justice in the morning and rescue the robbed from the oppressor, lest his wrath burn unquenched (vv. 11-12). Against a city confident in its rock and its walls, God says, I am against you, and will punish according to the fruit of their deeds, kindling a fire that devours everything around (vv. 13-14).
21.theology:
Prayer used as a last-resort lever by people unwilling to repent is refused (vv. 1-2; compare 14:11-12). God may turn the language of redemption against his own people: the outstretched arm that freed Israel now fights them (v. 5).

The choice of Deuteronomy is set again, but the way of life now runs through surrender (vv. 8-9; Deut 30:15-19; Matt 7:13-14). Judgment on a community and mercy to individuals within it stand together (vv. 9-10).

The first duty of God's appointed king is justice for the robbed and oppressed, before anything else in the day (v. 12); confidence in position and defences is answered by I am against you (v. 13), and each is repaid according to the fruit of his deeds (v. 14; 17:10).
21.examples:
Twenty years of ignoring the prophet, and then an official delegation when the siege lines go up.

Wanting Hezekiah's outcome without Hezekiah's posture.

The exodus arm stretched out the other way.

A way of life that looks exactly like treason.

Justice done before breakfast, or not at all.

"Who shall come down against us?" answered by "I am against you."

22.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word,<sup>2</sup>and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place.<sup>4</sup>For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people.<sup>5</sup>But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.<sup>6</sup>For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city.<sup>7</sup>I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire.<sup>8</sup>"'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?"<sup>9</sup>And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"<sup>10</sup>Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land.<sup>11</sup>For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more,<sup>12</sup>but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."<sup>13</sup>"Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages,<sup>14</sup>who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion.<sup>15</sup>Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him.<sup>16</sup>He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.<sup>17</sup>But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."<sup>18</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!'<sup>19</sup>With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem."<sup>20</sup>"Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed.<sup>21</sup>I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.<sup>22</sup>The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil.<sup>23</sup>O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"<sup>24</sup>"As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off<sup>25</sup>and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans.<sup>26</sup>I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die.<sup>27</sup>But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."<sup>28</sup>Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know?<sup>29</sup>O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!<sup>30</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Do Justice, or This House Becomes a Desolation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is sent down to the palace (vv. 1-2): Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, with no wrong to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow (v. 3). Obey, and kings will keep riding through these gates (v. 4); refuse, and I swear by myself that this house shall become a desolation (v. 5). Though the palace is like Gilead and Lebanon, its cedars will be cut and burned (vv. 6-7), and passing nations will ask why, and be told: Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The throne is held on terms, and the terms are the treatment of people who cannot defend themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word, and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates. Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place. For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word, and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates.

The prophet is sent to the palace, and told to preach at the gate again — the same method as the temple sermon (7:2) and the Sabbath sermon (17:19). He addresses the king, the civil service and the public together, because all three are implicated in how a country is run.

Note the title: who sits on the throne of David. Everything that follows is measured against what that throne was for.

Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place.

Here is the royal job description, and it is strikingly concrete. Not defend the borders, not maintain the temple, not manage the economy: deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. Get the stolen thing back. And protect the same three groups God names every time — the immigrant, the orphan, the widow — the people with no family power to protect them.

This is not a political programme read back into Scripture; it is the charter of Israel's monarchy, and the prophets judge every king by it.

For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.

The same two futures as chapter 17, and the same door: obedience keeps the dynasty riding through these gates; refusal empties the palace.

And God binds himself to it: I swear by myself. There is nothing higher to swear by. The promise to David was never a licence for his descendants to behave as they liked.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city. I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire. "'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?" And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city.

The palace is compared to the most impressive landscapes the region had: the wooded highlands of Gilead, the cedar summits of Lebanon. Partly this is about the building itself, which was panelled with imported cedar, and partly about how the dynasty looked to everyone — solid, green, permanent.

The ESV notes that an uninhabited city is in Hebrew "cities". Either way, what looked like a forest becomes desert.

I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire.

The image turns from forest to logging camp. God will prepare destroyers — literally commission them, as one hires woodcutters — and the cedars the king was so proud of will be firewood.

Anything built to display our own permanence is, in the end, timber.

"'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?" And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"

The ruins will preach. Travellers will ask the question, and the answer will be public and accurate — not bad luck, not the superior power of Babylon's gods, but a broken covenant.

Israel was called to make God known among the nations. She does it here, from the rubble, and the sermon is true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Woe to Him Who Builds by Unrighteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Weep not for him who is dead, but for Shallum, carried off, who shall return here no more (vv. 10-12). Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, using his neighbour's labour and paying nothing (v. 13), panelling in cedar and painting in vermilion (v. 14). Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? His father ate and drank and did justice and righteousness, and it was well with him; he judged the cause of the poor and needy: Is not this to know me? (vv. 15-16). But this king's eyes and heart are set on dishonest gain and innocent blood (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Knowing God is defined, in God's own words, as judging the cause of the poor and needy.

verseByVerse.quote: Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land. For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more, but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land.

A funeral instruction that reverses the usual grief. The dead man is Josiah, killed at Megiddo, and the whole country mourned him. God says: stop weeping for the king who died in his own land and start weeping for the one being marched away alive.

There are worse things than dying at home. Josiah was spared what is coming (2 Kgs 22:20); his son was not.

For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more, but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."

Shallum is Jehoahaz, who reigned three months before Pharaoh deposed him and took him to Egypt. Three of the four kings in this chapter end their lives in a foreign country.

Twice in one sentence: He shall return here no more, and he shall never see this land again. Exile is not only punishment; it is the specific loss of home.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages, who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion. Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him. He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD. But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages,

Now Jehoiakim, and the charge is unpaid labour. He is building a palace during a national crisis, and he is doing it with forced work: makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages.

The law was emphatic that a labourer's pay must not be held overnight, because the poor live day to day. James says the wages cry out and the cries reach God's ears. God notices payroll.

who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion.

Listen to the king's own voice: I will build myself a great house. The details are the details of a brochure — spacious rooms, large windows, cedar panelling, expensive red paint.

Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him. He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.

The question cuts through everything: Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Kingship is not a building project or a standard of living.

Then Josiah is held up, and notice how ordinary the description is. Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? He enjoyed his life; there is no asceticism here. And twice comes the refrain: it was well with him, and then it was well.

And then the sentence that should stop every religious reader: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me?

God defines the knowledge of himself by the treatment of the poor. Not instead of worship, prayer or doctrine — this book has spent twenty chapters on idolatry — but as inseparable from them. A man who defends the cause of people who cannot pay him knows God; a man who does not, whatever else he knows, does not know him.

But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."

Eyes and heart only: attention and affection both fixed on the take. That is a portrait of a man whose inner life has narrowed to one thing, and the consequences run outward into blood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Burial of a Donkey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Of Jehoiakim: no one will lament him with Ah, my brother! or Ah, his majesty! (v. 18); With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem (v. 19). Judah is told to cry from the mountains, for all your lovers are destroyed (v. 20). I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth (v. 21); her shepherds will be shepherded by the wind (v. 22), and the city nested in cedar will groan like a woman in labour (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The king who built the finest house in Jerusalem is dragged out of the city gate like a dead animal.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!' With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem." "Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed. I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice. The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil. O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!'

The funeral cries of that world are quoted and cancelled. Nobody will say the family words, and nobody will say the court words. The man who spent his reign building a monument will get no ceremony at all.

With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem."

A dead donkey is hauled out of the city and left. That is the burial of the king of Judah: dragged and dumped.

Set it beside the cedar and the vermilion. The house he built to be remembered by, and no grave anyone would visit.

"Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed.

The city is told to climb the high places in every direction and shout — north to Lebanon, north-east to Bashan, south-east to Abarim — and everywhere the news is the same. All your lovers are destroyed: the allies courted since chapter 2 are gone.

I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.

Here is one of the saddest diagnoses in the book. God spoke in your prosperity — while things were going well, when listening would have cost nothing and prevented everything. Good times are when warnings are cheapest to heed and hardest to hear.

The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil. O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"

A bitter joke: the shepherds who were supposed to lead the flock will themselves be herded, and by the wind. And the city nested among the cedars — comfortable, elevated, expensively furnished — will cry out like a woman in labour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — The Signet Ring Torn Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off (v. 24), and hand him to Nebuchadnezzar (v. 25); he and his mother will be hurled into another country and die there (vv. 26-27). Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? (v. 28). O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD! (v. 29): Write this man down as childless, for no offspring of his will sit on David's throne (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: The signet ring of the house of David is pulled off and thrown away, and the line looks finished.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans. I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die. But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off

Coniah is Jehoiachin, eighteen years old, three months on the throne, deported to Babylon in 597 BC.

A signet ring was a king's identity: it carried his seal, it went everywhere with him, it was never taken off. To call the Davidic king the signet on God's right hand is to say he is God's own authority displayed in the world.

And God says he would tear you off. The verb is violent. Even the most intimate symbol of the covenant with David is not immune when the man wearing it is faithless.

and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans. I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die. But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."

Four times into the hand, and the last phrase is the ache of every exile: the land to which they will long to return. The longing is granted and the return is not.

His mother goes with him, as 13:18 said she would. History records that Jehoiachin lived thirty-seven years in Babylon and was eventually released to eat at the king's table — the note on which the book of Kings closes, and a flicker of light at the end of that history.

verseByVerse.quote: Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know? O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD! Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know?

The question echoes the broken flask of chapter 19. A pot that has been smashed is swept up and thrown out without a thought, and that is what happened to the king: a vessel no one cares for.

O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!

Three times, like a herald in the street. The land itself is summoned to hear what is about to be said about the house of David.

Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."

Enter it in the record: childless. He had sons, but for the purposes of the throne the line stops here. No descendant of Jehoiachin will reign in Jerusalem, and none ever did.

That looks like the end of the promise to David, and for centuries it hung there.

Two things happen afterwards, and hold them together. First, Haggai takes this very image and gives it back: to Zerubbabel, Jehoiachin's grandson, God says, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you (Hag 2:23). The ring torn off is put back on.

Second, Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy that runs straight through this cursed name: Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon, and then Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel (Matt 1:11-12) — and on to Joseph, the husband of Mary.

Jesus is the legal heir of David through Jehoiachin, and he is not Joseph's biological son. The line that carried the throne also carried the curse, and the King who finally sat on David's throne came into that family without coming from that seed. What God said stands, and what God promised stands, and the gospel is how both are true at once.

22.title: The House of David on Trial
22.overview:
Jeremiah is sent to the palace with the royal charter: do justice, rescue the robbed from the oppressor, protect the immigrant, the orphan and the widow, shed no innocent blood (vv. 1-3). Obey and the dynasty rides on; refuse and God swears the house will be a desolation, its cedars cut and burned, while passing nations are told the reason was a forsaken covenant (vv. 4-9).

Weep not for the dead king but for Shallum, deported and never to return (vv. 10-12). Woe to Jehoiakim, who built a cedar palace with unpaid labour: his father ate and drank and judged the cause of the poor and needy — Is not this to know me? — while this king's eyes and heart are on dishonest gain (vv. 13-17). He will have the burial of a donkey (vv. 18-19). Judah is told to cry out from the mountains, for God spoke in her prosperity and she would not listen (vv. 20-23).

Finally Coniah: though he were the signet ring on God's right hand, he would be torn off and hurled into a foreign country to die there, a broken pot no one cares for, to be written down as childless, none of his offspring sitting on David's throne (vv. 24-30).
22.theology:
The Davidic throne is held on covenant terms, and the test is justice for those who cannot defend themselves (vv. 3-5). God defines the knowledge of himself by the judging of the cause of the poor and needy (v. 16) — inseparable from, not a substitute for, true worship.

God speaks to people in their prosperity, when heeding him is cheapest, and that is when refusal is most characteristic (v. 21). Grandeur built on injustice ends as firewood and an unmourned burial (vv. 7, 19).

Not even the signet ring of David's house is immune (v. 24), and the line is declared finished (v. 30). Yet God gives the signet back to Zerubbabel (Hag 2:23), and Matthew traces Christ's legal descent through this very name (Matt 1:11-12) — the curse standing and the promise kept.
22.examples:
A king judged by whether a robbed man can get his property back.

Cedar panelling and vermilion paint, paid for with wages never handed over.

"Is not this to know me?" said about the cause of the poor.

A dead donkey dragged out of the gate, and that is the state funeral.

God speaking while things are going well, and being told: I will not listen.

A signet ring torn off — and put back on a grandson's hand.

Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply.<sup>4</sup>I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.<sup>6</sup>In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'<sup>7</sup>"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they shall no longer say, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,'<sup>8</sup>but 'As the LORD lives who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' Then they shall dwell in their own land."<sup>9</sup>Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words.<sup>10</sup>For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right.<sup>11</sup>"Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.<sup>13</sup>In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray.<sup>14</sup>But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah."<sup>15</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."<sup>16</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'"<sup>18</sup>For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened?<sup>19</sup>Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked.<sup>20</sup>The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.<sup>21</sup>"I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.<sup>22</sup>But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds.<sup>23</sup>"Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away?<sup>24</sup>Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD.<sup>25</sup>I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, 'I have dreamed, I have dreamed!'<sup>26</sup>How long shall there be lies in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and who prophesy the deceit of their own heart,<sup>27</sup>who think to make my people forget my name by their dreams that they tell one another, even as their fathers forgot my name for Baal?<sup>28</sup>Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD.<sup>29</sup>Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?<sup>30</sup>Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another.<sup>31</sup>Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.'<sup>32</sup>Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.<sup>33</sup>"When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.'<sup>34</sup>And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household.<sup>35</sup>Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'<sup>36</sup>But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God.<sup>37</sup>Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'<sup>38</sup>But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'"<sup>39</sup>therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers.<sup>40</sup>And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! (v. 1): they have not attended to the flock, so God will attend to them (v. 2). He will gather the remnant himself and set over them shepherds who care, so that none is missing (vv. 3-4). Behold, the days are coming when he will raise up for David a righteous Branch who will execute justice and righteousness in the land (v. 5), in whose days Judah is saved, and this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness' (v. 6). Then the oath will be by the God who brought Israel out of the north country (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Against every failed shepherd God sets one King who will do what the house of David was given the throne to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!" declares the LORD. Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds who care for my people: "You have scattered my flock and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD. Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply. I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!" declares the LORD.

The shepherds are the kings and leaders of chapter 22, and the charge is precise. They did not merely fail to gather; they destroy and scatter. Bad leadership is not neutral.

And notice whose sheep they are: the sheep of my pasture. The flock was never theirs. That is the reason the woe is so heavy — they mishandled someone else's property, and the owner was watching.

Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds who care for my people: "You have scattered my flock and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD.

There is a grim play on words here. They did not attend to the flock, so God will attend to them. The visitation they neglected to make will be made on them.

Anyone with pastoral responsibility should feel the weight of it: the opposite of caring for people is not cruelty but inattention, and God treats inattention as an evil deed.

Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply.

And now God takes the job himself: I will gather. Ezekiel puts it even more strongly: Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out (Ezek 34:11). When human shepherds fail, God does not abandon the flock; he comes for them personally.

I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.

Then he gives them shepherds again — a promise fulfilled in the pastors and teachers Christ gives his church, and finally in the chief Shepherd himself (1 Pet 5:4). And the measure of the new arrangement is a shepherd's measure: neither shall any be missing. Every sheep accounted for.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.

Chapter 22 ended with the royal line written down as childless. Here is the answer, and the timing is deliberate.

A righteous Branch. The image is of a shoot growing from a stump — a tree cut down to the ground, and one living green shoot coming up out of it. Isaiah had used it: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit (Isa 11:1). The dynasty is a felled tree; God will grow a king out of the stump.

And what he will do is exactly what chapter 22 demanded and no king delivered: execute justice and righteousness in the land. The job description is unchanged; at last there is someone to fill it.

In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'

The name is the summit of the book so far. Zedekiah, the king reigning as Jeremiah spoke, had a name meaning "the LORD is my righteousness" — and he was a weak, faithless man whose reign ended in fire. The coming King will carry the name truly, and with one change: not my but our.

Think about what that means. The King's name is a statement about his people's standing. He is called what they receive. His righteousness is reckoned as theirs, which is why they are saved and dwell securely in his days rather than in their own.

The New Testament says it in plain prose. The righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe (Rom 3:21-22). Christ became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30). For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21).

Everything Jeremiah has exposed — the deceitful heart, the leopard's spots, the sin engraved with an iron pen — requires a righteousness from outside. Here is his name.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they shall no longer say, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' but 'As the LORD lives who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' Then they shall dwell in their own land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they shall no longer say, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' but 'As the LORD lives who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' Then they shall dwell in their own land."

The new-exodus oath of 16:14-15 is repeated, and its position here is the point: it comes immediately after the righteous Branch. The greater rescue and the greater King belong together.

The ESV notes a small textual difference in verse 8. The substance is unaffected: the God who is bringing them home will be known by that, as he was once known by the Red Sea.

Christians read this with the knowledge that the return from Babylon, when it came, was modest — a few thousand people, a small temple, no king. The oath still waits for its full weight, and it finds it in a rescue out of a deeper exile than Babylon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Both Prophet and Priest Are Ungodly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake, says Jeremiah, because of the LORD and because of his holy words (v. 9). The land mourns under a curse (v. 10); Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil (v. 11), so their way will be slippery paths in the dark (v. 12). Samaria's prophets prophesied by Baal; Jerusalem's are worse — they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil (vv. 13-14) — and they will be fed bitter food, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Preaching that comforts people in their sin is not a minor failure; it is the source from which a nation's ungodliness spreads.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words. For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right. "Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD. Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words.

Before he says a word against the false prophets, Jeremiah describes what God's word does to him: heart broken, bones shaking, unsteady on his feet like a drunk. Not because of the opposition — because of the LORD and because of his holy words.

That is the contrast the whole section turns on. Here is a man wrecked by handling the word of God, about to describe men who handle it lightly and sleep well.

For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right.

The drought is still on, and it is read theologically: the land mourns because of the curse. And the charge against the leadership is a phrase worth remembering: their might is not right. They have power and use it wrongly.

"Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD.

Even in my house. Not only in the streets and the high places — inside the temple, among the men conducting the worship. Corruption at the centre of religion is worse than corruption outside it, because there is nowhere left for a seeker to go.

Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.

Men who gave others no light will walk in the dark on wet stone. The punishment fits.

verseByVerse.quote: In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray. But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah." Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray.

Samaria is the northern kingdom, destroyed a century before, and its prophets were openly pagan. God calls that an unsavory thing — repellent, but at least undisguised.

But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah."

And the men in Jerusalem, who preach in the name of the LORD, are worse: a horrible thing. Their private lives are corrupt and their public message is false, and the two are connected.

The phrase to weigh is they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil. That is the effect of their preaching, and it is the exact opposite of a prophet's job. A man goes to church intending to break with something, hears that God is fine with it, and goes home reinforced.

Judged by outcome rather than intention, that is more destructive than Baal worship, because it uses God's own name to do it.

Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."

The diet of 9:15, now served to the preachers. And the reason names them as the source: ungodliness did not seep up from the people to the pulpit; it flowed out from the pulpit into the country.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Visions of Their Own Minds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not listen to the words of the prophets, who fill people with vain hopes and speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD (v. 16), telling those who despise God's word, It shall be well with you (v. 17). None of them has stood in the council of the LORD (v. 18), and the storm of the LORD is already breaking (vv. 19-20). I did not send the prophets, yet they ran (v. 21); had they stood in his council they would have turned them from their evil way (v. 22). And no one hides from a God who fills heaven and earth (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: The test of preaching is not sincerity or eloquence but whether it comes from God and turns people from evil.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD. They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'" For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened? Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked. The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.

A direct instruction to the congregation: Do not listen. Hearers are responsible for what they sit under.

And the mechanism is named again (14:14): visions of their own minds. Not fabrication in the crude sense — these men very likely believed their own material. Sincerity is not the test. Origin is: not from the mouth of the LORD.

They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'"

Here is the content of the false message in two sentences, and notice the audiences: people who despise the word of the LORD and people who stubbornly follow their own hearts. To exactly those people they say, all will be well.

Paul saw the same market forming: the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim 4:3).

For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened?

The test is put as a question about the council chamber. A true prophet has stood where God's decisions are made and has listened. These men never went in, which is why they can only report their own minds.

Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked. The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.

While they promise fair weather, the storm is already moving. And the last line is honest about timing: In the latter days you will understand it clearly. Some things only make sense afterwards, and the people telling you otherwise now will not be there to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds. "Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away? Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.

Two flat denials with two energetic verbs. They ran; they prophesied. Zeal and output are not evidence of a call. It is possible to be extremely busy in ministry that God never commissioned.

But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds.

And here is the practical test, and it is a wonderfully usable one. Preaching that comes from God turns people from evil. That is its fruit.

Not that everyone repents — Jeremiah's own ministry is proof that faithful preaching can be widely rejected. But the aim and the tendency of the word is to turn people, and a message whose effect is to leave everyone exactly as they were, comfortable and unchallenged, has already told you where it came from. Deuteronomy gave a test by fulfilment (Deut 18:21-22); Jeremiah adds a test by fruit.

"Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away? Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD.

The false prophets have been behaving as though God were local and short-sighted: a deity of the temple precinct who does not hear what is said in private. God answers with three questions that fill the sky.

The psalm turns the same truth into comfort: Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (Ps 139:7). To a liar it is terror; to a child it is home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has heard the prophets who cry I have dreamed, I have dreamed! (v. 25) and prophesy the deceit of their own heart (v. 26), making his people forget his name as their fathers forgot it for Baal (v. 27). Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? (v. 28). Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces? (v. 29). Three times: I am against the prophets who steal words, use their tongues, and tell lying dreams (vv. 30-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Dreams and God's word are not two grades of the same thing; they are straw and wheat.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, 'I have dreamed, I have dreamed!' How long shall there be lies in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and who prophesy the deceit of their own heart, who think to make my people forget my name by their dreams that they tell one another, even as their fathers forgot my name for Baal? Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD. Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, 'I have dreamed, I have dreamed!' How long shall there be lies in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and who prophesy the deceit of their own heart,

The repetition mimics them: I have dreamed, I have dreamed! — the excited claim of a private revelation that cannot be checked. And God traces it to its source, which is the heart of chapter 17: the deceit is in the prophets' own hearts, and they are its first victims.

who think to make my people forget my name by their dreams that they tell one another, even as their fathers forgot my name for Baal?

Their dreams have the same effect as Baal did: they make people forget God's name. Ministry that draws attention to the minister's experiences is not neutral; it crowds out the name it claims to serve.

Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD.

The ruling is not that dreams must be suppressed. Tell the dream, and call it a dream. What is forbidden is passing it off as the word of God.

And the comparison settles it: What has straw in common with wheat? Both come off the same field; one feeds people and one does not. Preaching that is mostly the preacher's own material may be pleasant, but nobody lives on straw.

Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?

Here is what the real thing does. It burns, as it burned in Jeremiah's bones when he tried to keep silent (20:9); and it breaks rock, which is the only hope for a people whose faces are harder than rock (5:3).

If preaching never burns or breaks anything, the problem may not be the congregation.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another. Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.' Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another.

Three times God says I am against the prophets, and each names a different fraud.

The first is plagiarism: they steal my words from one another. Having nothing from God themselves, they recycle each other's material. A prophetic culture can run for years on borrowed phrases with no fresh dealing with God behind any of it.

Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.'

The second is the formula. They have learned the phrase that makes speech sound authoritative and they attach it to their own opinions. The verse is almost comic in its precision: they use their tongues and say, declares the LORD.

Every generation has its version — a tone of voice, a way of quoting, a confident "God told me" — by which personal judgement is given divine weight.

Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.

The third is recklessness. Note the word: not only malice but carelessness with other people's souls. And the verdict is quietly devastating: they do not profit this people at all. All that ministry, and nobody was helped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–40 — The Burden of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When people ask What is the burden of the LORD?, the answer is You are the burden, and I will cast you off (v. 33). Anyone still using the phrase will be punished (v. 34); they are to ask instead, What has the LORD answered? or What has the LORD spoken? (vv. 35-37), for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God (v. 36). Those who persist will be lifted up and cast away, with everlasting reproach and perpetual shame (vv. 38-40).
verseByVerse.theology: A reverent-sounding phrase had become a joke about God's word, and God takes the joke away.

verseByVerse.quote: "When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.' And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household. Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God. Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'" therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers. And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.'

This last section turns on a word. The Hebrew term rendered burden was a standard label for a prophetic oracle, and it also means a load. People had started asking Jeremiah, with a smirk, what today's burden was — treating God's word as a heavy, tiresome thing and the prophet as the man who carries it round.

God takes the joke and returns it: You are the burden, and I will cast you off. The ESV notes a textual variation in the question, but the wordplay is plain enough. You think my word is a weight? You are the weight, and I am putting it down.

And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household.

The phrase is banned, and the ban reaches everyone — prophet, priest, ordinary citizen. It is a striking example of God legislating against a piece of religious slang because of the attitude packed into it.

Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'

And he gives them the replacement wording, which is humble and expectant: What has the LORD answered? Not, what is today's burden, but what has God said. The change of phrase is a change of posture.

But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God.

Here is the heart of it: the burden is every man's own word. Everyone had made his own opinion the oracle. And the charge is the gravest in the chapter — you pervert the words of the living God: twisting them until they say something else.

Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'" therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers.

The sentence uses their own word against them one last time: they called God's message a burden, so he will lift you up like a load and put it down outside. The ESV notes that the phrase may be rendered "surely forget you".

And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"

The chapter that gave us the most beautiful name in the book — The LORD is our righteousness — ends with everlasting reproach for those who made his word a joke. The two belong together: the King who is our righteousness is the Word made flesh, and how people handle the word is finally how they handle him.

23.title: The Righteous Branch: The LORD Is Our Righteousness
23.overview:
Woe to the shepherds who scatter God's flock and do not attend to them: he will attend to them, gather the remnant himself, and set over them shepherds who care, so that none is missing (vv. 1-4). Then the promise: he will raise up for David a righteous Branch who will reign wisely and execute justice, in whose days Judah will be saved, and whose name is The LORD is our righteousness (vv. 5-6). The oath will one day be sworn by the God who brought Israel out of the north country (vv. 7-8).

Jeremiah is shaken to the bones by God's holy words (v. 9). Prophet and priest are ungodly, found out even in God's house (vv. 10-12); Jerusalem's prophets are worse than Samaria's, for they strengthen the hands of evildoers so that no one turns, and from them ungodliness has spread through the land (vv. 13-15).

The people are told not to listen to men who speak visions of their own minds and promise peace to those who despise God's word (vv. 16-17).
