None of them has stood in God's council (v. 18); the storm is already moving (vv. 19-20); God never sent them, and had they stood in his council they would have turned people from evil (vv. 21-22). No one can hide from a God who fills heaven and earth (vv. 23-24). Let the dreamer tell his dream, but God's word is wheat, not straw, and it burns like fire and breaks rock (vv. 25-29). Three times God declares himself against these prophets (vv. 30-32). Finally he bans the phrase the burden of the LORD, by which they had made his word a joke, and promises everlasting reproach to those who persist (vv. 33-40).
23.theology:
Leaders are accountable for a flock that belongs to God, and inattention is itself an evil deed (vv. 1-2). When shepherds fail, God gathers his people himself (v. 3; Ezek 34:11) and gives them true shepherds under the chief Shepherd (v. 4; 1 Pet 5:4; John 10:11).

The righteous Branch is the messianic King who does what David's house failed to do, and his name declares what his people receive: The LORD is our righteousness (vv. 5-6) — the imputed righteousness of Rom 3:21-22; 1 Cor 1:30; 2 Cor 5:21.

False prophecy is sincere, energetic and self-derived (vv. 16, 21), and is tested not by eloquence but by origin and fruit: God's word turns people from evil (v. 22; Deut 18:20-22). It is wheat, not straw, and it burns and breaks (vv. 28-29). Hearers are responsible for what they listen to (v. 16; 2 Tim 4:3-4), and to treat God's word as a burden is to invite being set down as one (vv. 33-40).
23.examples:
The opposite of caring for people is not cruelty but inattention.

A shoot growing out of a stump that everyone had written off.

A King whose name states his people's standing, not his own.

Going to church intending to break with something, and going home reinforced.

Preachers recycling each other's material with nothing fresh from God.

Straw and wheat off the same field: one of them feeds people.

24.text: <sup>1</sup>After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."<sup>4</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>5</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.<sup>6</sup>I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up.<sup>7</sup>I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.<sup>8</sup>"But thus says the LORD: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them.<sup>10</sup>And I will send sword, famine, and pestilence upon them, until they shall be utterly destroyed from the land that I gave to them and their fathers."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Two Baskets Before the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After Nebuchadnezzar had deported Jeconiah with the officials, craftsmen and metal workers, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD (v. 1). One holds very good figs, like first-ripe figs, the other very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten (v. 2). What do you see, Jeremiah?, God asks, and he answers exactly what is in front of him (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Two baskets at the temple door, and the sorting is not the one anybody in Jerusalem would have made.

verseByVerse.quote: After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD. One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten. And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD.

The date fixes everything. This is after 597 BC, when Babylon took the young king Jeconiah — the Coniah of chapter 22 — along with the court, the skilled workers and the metalworkers. The first deportation has happened, and Jerusalem is still standing with Zedekiah on the throne.

That situation produced a very natural theology in the city: God has judged those people and spared us. The deportees must have been the sinners. We are the survivors, we still have the temple, and that proves whose side God is on.

So the vision is set before the temple, in the very place where that theology was preached, and it is a picture of the harvest offering: two baskets of figs brought to God's house.

One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten.

First-ripe figs, picked in June, were a delicacy — the best of the crop. The other basket is not mediocre fruit but rotten: so bad that they could not be eaten. There is no middle category anywhere in this chapter.

And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."

The question is the one from the almond branch and the boiling pot (1:11, 13). God's method with this prophet is to make him look at something ordinary and say what is there, and then to tell him what it means. Jeremiah's answer is simply accurate, and it commits him to nothing — which is why what follows lands so hard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–7 — The Good Figs: the Exiles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans (vv. 4-5). I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up (v. 6). I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The people who lost everything are the good figs, and God promises to give them the one thing they cannot give themselves: a heart to know him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans. I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up. I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.

The good figs are the people in Babylon.

That reverses everything Jerusalem believed. The men in chains, who lost their homes, their positions and their temple, are the first-ripe fruit. And note the phrase whom I have sent away: God, not Nebuchadnezzar, sent them. Their deportation was not abandonment but transplanting.

It is a hard lesson for comfortable believers. Circumstances are not a scoreboard. The people whose lives look broken may be the ones God has his eye on, and the ones still holding the property may be the rotten basket.

I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up.

Listen to the verbs: build, plant, and the refusal of tear down and pluck up. They are the four verbs of Jeremiah's call (1:10), and here the two constructive ones stand on their own, with the destructive pair expressly set aside. Ruin is not the last word of this ministry, and the exiles are where the building starts.

I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart."

And here is the promise the whole book has been driving toward. Chapter 13 asked whether a leopard could change its spots; chapter 17 said the heart is deceitful and unsearchable. The answer is not better instruction: I will give them a heart to know me.

God gives what he requires. Ezekiel says the same: I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh (Ezek 11:19). And the covenant formula follows, as it always does: they shall be my people and I will be their God.

Notice the order in the last clause. Because he gives the heart, they shall return to me with their whole heart. Their wholehearted return is real, and it is the fruit of his gift rather than the price of it. That is the shape of the new covenant in 31:31-34, and of every conversion since.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Bad Figs: Those Who Remain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt (v. 8). They will become a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse wherever they are driven (v. 9), and sword, famine and pestilence will pursue them until they are gone from the land (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Keeping your place in the land turns out to prove nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "But thus says the LORD: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt. I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them. And I will send sword, famine, and pestilence upon them, until they shall be utterly destroyed from the land that I gave to them and their fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But thus says the LORD: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt.

And the bad figs are the people still at home, with the king, the officials and the temple — plus the group who ran to Egypt rather than submit.

They were the ones who had drawn the comforting conclusion. They kept their houses, their jobs and their worship, and they took all of it as evidence of God's approval. God calls them uneatable fruit.

The warning for anyone reading is plain enough. Being spared a disaster that fell on others proves nothing about your standing with God, and it can be the most dangerous position of all if it is read as a verdict.

I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them.

Four words for public disgrace — reproach, byword, taunt, curse — and the ESV notes a small textual difficulty in the opening phrase. The nation called to make God's name known among the nations becomes the story other nations tell as a warning.

And I will send sword, famine, and pestilence upon them, until they shall be utterly destroyed from the land that I gave to them and their fathers."

The three-fold sentence of the book, and the last clause carries the sting: destroyed from the land that I gave to them. The very thing they were trusting in — possession of the land — is what they lose, because it was never a possession they had earned.

The chapter is ten verses long and it dismantles a whole way of reading providence. The exiles God had sent away were the ones he was watching for good; the survivors who felt vindicated were rotting in the basket. Anyone tempted to measure God's favour by his circumstances should read it twice.

24.title: Two Baskets of Figs
24.overview:
After the deportation of Jeconiah and the leading men of Judah in 597 BC, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs set before the temple: one of first-ripe figs, one so rotten they cannot be eaten (vv. 1-3).

The good figs are the exiles in Babylon, whom God says he sent away. He will set his eyes on them for good, bring them back, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know him, so that they will be his people and return to him with their whole heart (vv. 4-7).

The bad figs are Zedekiah, his officials, those who remain in Jerusalem and those who fled to Egypt. They will become a horror, a reproach, a byword, a taunt and a curse wherever they are driven, pursued by sword, famine and pestilence until they are destroyed from the land God gave their fathers (vv. 8-10).
24.theology:
Circumstances are not a scoreboard of God's favour: those who lost everything are the good fruit, and those still holding house, throne and temple are the rotten basket (vv. 5, 8). Exile itself was God's act of transplanting, not abandonment (v. 5).

For the first time the constructive verbs of the call stand alone — build and plant, without tearing down (v. 6; 1:10).

God gives what he demands: a heart to know him (v. 7), answering the deceitful heart of 17:9 and the leopard's spots of 13:23, matching Ezek 11:19-20 and anticipating the new covenant of 31:31-34. Wholehearted return is the fruit of that gift, not its price.
24.examples:
Two baskets at the temple door, sorted the opposite way to the city's theology.

Reading your own survival as a verdict in your favour.

Deportation described as transplanting.

Build and plant, for once with no tearing down attached.

Being given the heart you were told to produce.

25.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (that was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon),<sup>2</sup>which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem:<sup>3</sup>"For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day, the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened.<sup>4</sup>You have neither listened nor inclined your ears to hear, although the LORD persistently sent to you all his servants the prophets,<sup>5</sup>saying, 'Turn now, every one of you, from his evil way and evil deeds, and dwell upon the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers from of old and forever.<sup>6</sup>Do not go after other gods to serve and worship them, or provoke me to anger with the work of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.'<sup>7</sup>Yet you have not listened to me, declares the LORD, that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm.<sup>8</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: Because you have not obeyed my words,<sup>9</sup>behold, I will send for all the tribes of the north, declares the LORD, and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and its inhabitants, and against all these surrounding nations. I will devote them to destruction, and make them a horror, a hissing, and an everlasting desolation.<sup>10</sup>Moreover, I will banish from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp.<sup>11</sup>This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.<sup>12</sup>Then after seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their iniquity, declares the LORD, making the land an everlasting waste.<sup>13</sup>I will bring upon that land all the words that I have uttered against it, everything written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.<sup>14</sup>For many nations and great kings shall make slaves even of them, and I will recompense them according to their deeds and the work of their hands."<sup>15</sup>Thus the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it.<sup>16</sup>They shall drink and stagger and be crazed because of the sword that I am sending among them."<sup>17</sup>So I took the cup from the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to whom the LORD sent me drink it:<sup>18</sup>Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials, to make them a desolation and a waste, a hissing and a curse, as at this day;<sup>19</sup>Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, all his people,<sup>20</sup>and all the mixed tribes among them; all the kings of the land of Uz and all the kings of the land of the Philistines (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod);<sup>21</sup>Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon;<sup>22</sup>all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the coastland across the sea;<sup>23</sup>Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair;<sup>24</sup>all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert;<sup>25</sup>all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of Media;<sup>26</sup>all the kings of the north, far and near, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth. And after them the king of Babylon shall drink.<sup>27</sup>"Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink, be drunk and vomit, fall and rise no more, because of the sword that I am sending among you.'<sup>28</sup>"And if they refuse to accept the cup from your hand to drink, then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: You must drink!<sup>29</sup>For behold, I begin to work disaster at the city that is called by my name, and shall you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, for I am summoning a sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of hosts.'<sup>30</sup>"You, therefore, shall prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: "'The LORD will roar from on high, and from his holy habitation utter his voice; he will roar mightily against his fold, and shout, like those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth.<sup>31</sup>The clamor will resound to the ends of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against the nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh, and the wicked he will put to the sword, declares the LORD.'<sup>32</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, disaster is going forth from nation to nation, and a great tempest is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth!<sup>33</sup>"And those pierced by the LORD on that day shall extend from one end of the earth to the other. They shall not be lamented, or gathered, or buried; they shall be dung on the surface of the ground.<sup>34</sup>"Wail, you shepherds, and cry out, and roll in ashes, you lords of the flock, for the days of your slaughter and dispersion have come, and you shall fall like a choice vessel.<sup>35</sup>No refuge will remain for the shepherds, nor escape for the lords of the flock.<sup>36</sup>A voice—the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock! For the LORD is laying waste their pasture,<sup>37</sup>and the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the LORD.<sup>38</sup>Like a lion he has left his lair, for their land has become a waste because of the sword of the oppressor, and because of his fierce anger."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim (vv. 1-2) Jeremiah sums up his ministry: For twenty-three years the word has come and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened (v. 3). God also persistently sent to you all his servants the prophets (v. 4), saying, Turn now, every one of you, from his evil way and evil deeds, and do not go after other gods, Then I will do you no harm (vv. 5-6). Yet you have not listened, to their own harm (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-three years of preaching, summarised by the prophet himself in one word: unheard.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (that was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon), which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem: "For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day, the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened. You have neither listened nor inclined your ears to hear, although the LORD persistently sent to you all his servants the prophets, saying, 'Turn now, every one of you, from his evil way and evil deeds, and dwell upon the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers from of old and forever. Do not go after other gods to serve and worship them, or provoke me to anger with the work of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.' Yet you have not listened to me, declares the LORD, that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (that was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon),

The date is 605 BC, the year Babylon beat Egypt at Carchemish and became the power of the age. It is also the year of the scroll in chapter 36. The world has just changed shape, and Jeremiah has been preaching into it for over two decades.

which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem: "For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day, the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened.

He counts the years aloud: twenty-three. From his call (1:2) to this moment, and the summary of the whole period is five words — but you have not listened.

Take that seriously before drawing any lesson from it. Twenty-three years of faithful, costly, unpopular work with no visible result. If ministry is measured by response, this is a failed career; the man himself would have said so in chapter 20. What God asked of him was faithfulness, and the record is that he was persistent for as long as it took.

You have neither listened nor inclined your ears to hear, although the LORD persistently sent to you all his servants the prophets,

And he was not alone: God persistently sent prophets, plural, over centuries (7:25). The same word is used of God's sending and of Jeremiah's speaking. Patience is measured here in messengers.

saying, 'Turn now, every one of you, from his evil way and evil deeds, and dwell upon the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers from of old and forever. Do not go after other gods to serve and worship them, or provoke me to anger with the work of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.'

Here is the entire prophetic message in three sentences: turn, don't serve other gods, and you may stay. The offer at the end is almost startling in its simplicity — Then I will do you no harm. Everything that follows in this chapter was avoidable to the last week.

Yet you have not listened to me, declares the LORD, that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm.

And the closing phrase names who loses: to your own harm. As in 7:19, the provocation lands on the provoker.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because they have not obeyed, God will send for the tribes of the north and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant (vv. 8-9); he will banish the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp (v. 10). These nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years (v. 11), and then God will punish Babylon itself (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The empire that executes the judgment is called God's servant, and is given a term that expires.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: Because you have not obeyed my words, behold, I will send for all the tribes of the north, declares the LORD, and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and its inhabitants, and against all these surrounding nations. I will devote them to destruction, and make them a horror, a hissing, and an everlasting desolation. Moreover, I will banish from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp. This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: Because you have not obeyed my words, behold, I will send for all the tribes of the north, declares the LORD, and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and its inhabitants, and against all these surrounding nations. I will devote them to destruction, and make them a horror, a hissing, and an everlasting desolation.

Two words carry the theology of this chapter. The first is I will send for — God summons the invader like a master calling a servant into the room.

The second is the title: Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant. A pagan emperor who worshipped Marduk, who will burn God's temple, is called God's servant. He does not know it, he does not intend it, and he will be judged for how he does it (v. 12) — and he is still the instrument in God's hand.

That is a hard and necessary doctrine. God governs the powers that hurt his people. It does not make their cruelty less culpable, and it does mean that history is not out of control.

Moreover, I will banish from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp.

The refrain of 7:34 and 16:9, with two homely details added: the sound of the hand-mill grinding grain at dawn, and the little oil lamp left burning at night in every house.

Those two are the sounds and sights of ordinary domestic life — breakfast being made, a light left on. That is what judgment takes away. Not first the palaces and armies: the kitchen and the lamp.

This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.

And here is the number that shaped the next century of faith: seventy years.

It is a sentence with an end date attached. The exile will be long — most who go will die there — and it is not endless. Daniel was reading this verse in Babylon when he worked out that the time was nearly up and began to pray (Dan 9:2). The Chronicler says the land kept its Sabbaths to fulfill seventy years (2 Chr 36:21).

God times his judgments. Hold on to that in a season that seems to have no end.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their iniquity, declares the LORD, making the land an everlasting waste. I will bring upon that land all the words that I have uttered against it, everything written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations. For many nations and great kings shall make slaves even of them, and I will recompense them according to their deeds and the work of their hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their iniquity, declares the LORD, making the land an everlasting waste.

The servant is judged too. Babylon's brutality was real brutality, freely chosen, and being useful to God's purposes is no defence — a truth already stated in 10:25 and worked out at length in chapters 50 and 51.

No one gets to plead that they were only the rod. The rod is answerable for being a rod.

I will bring upon that land all the words that I have uttered against it, everything written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.

A glimpse of the book itself: there is a written collection, and God treats what is written in it as what he will do. The scroll is not a record of opinions but a docket of decisions.

For many nations and great kings shall make slaves even of them, and I will recompense them according to their deeds and the work of their hands."

The phrase that has run through the book about Judah — repaid according to the work of their hands — is now applied to the empire. God uses one standard, and Paul states it as the rule of the final judgment: He will render to each one according to his works (Rom 2:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–29 — The Cup of the Wine of Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it (v. 15), until they stagger (v. 16). Jeremiah takes it to Jerusalem first (vv. 17-18), then to Egypt, the Philistines, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, Sidon, Arabia, Elam, Media and all the kingdoms of the earth — And after them the king of Babylon shall drink (vv. 19-26). They must Drink, be drunk and vomit, fall and rise no more (v. 27), and if they refuse, You must drink! (v. 28), For behold, I begin to work disaster at the city that is called by my name (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: God's own city drinks first, which settles for ever the question of whether he judges by favouritism.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it. They shall drink and stagger and be crazed because of the sword that I am sending among them." So I took the cup from the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to whom the LORD sent me drink it: Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials, to make them a desolation and a waste, a hissing and a curse, as at this day; Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, all his people, and all the mixed tribes among them; all the kings of the land of Uz and all the kings of the land of the Philistines (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod); Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon; all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the coastland across the sea; Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair; all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert; all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of Media; all the kings of the north, far and near, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth. And after them the king of Babylon shall drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it. They shall drink and stagger and be crazed because of the sword that I am sending among them."

A new vision, and one of the most important images in the Bible. God holds out a cup and tells his prophet to take it round the nations.

The picture works because everyone knows what strong drink does: it takes away balance, judgement and dignity, and the drinker cannot stop what happens next. The wrath of God is pictured not as a fit of temper but as a measured draught that a nation must drink to the bottom.

The image runs through Scripture. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps 75:8). Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem having drunk the cup of staggering (Isa 51:17). Habakkuk warns Babylon that The cup in the LORD's right hand will come around to you (Hab 2:16). Revelation says the worshippers of the beast will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger (Rev 14:10).

And then, in a garden, a man knelt and prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39). He knew exactly which cup it was, and he drank it to the dregs so that his people would never have to.

So I took the cup from the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to whom the LORD sent me drink it: Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials, to make them a desolation and a waste, a hissing and a curse, as at this day;

The order of the list is the sermon. Jerusalem drinks first. Not Egypt, not Babylon: the city with the temple in it.

Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, all his people, and all the mixed tribes among them; all the kings of the land of Uz and all the kings of the land of the Philistines (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod); Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon; all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the coastland across the sea; Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair; all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert; all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of Media; all the kings of the north, far and near, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth. And after them the king of Babylon shall drink.

The list moves outward in rings from Judah: Egypt to the south, the Philistine cities on the coast, the cousins east of the Jordan, the Phoenician ports, the desert tribes, the eastern empires — and ends with all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth.

Babylon comes last. The ESV notes that the Hebrew uses Sheshach, a code name for Babylon; at the moment of its greatest power, its name is written in cipher and placed at the end of the queue.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink, be drunk and vomit, fall and rise no more, because of the sword that I am sending among you.' "And if they refuse to accept the cup from your hand to drink, then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: You must drink! For behold, I begin to work disaster at the city that is called by my name, and shall you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, for I am summoning a sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of hosts.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink, be drunk and vomit, fall and rise no more, because of the sword that I am sending among you.'

The language is deliberately undignified. Empires that considered themselves eternal are pictured as a drunk in the street: sick, on the ground, unable to get up.

Scripture strips the glamour off power like this on purpose. The kingdoms whose armies emptied cities end the verse in their own vomit.

"And if they refuse to accept the cup from your hand to drink, then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: You must drink!

Refusal is anticipated and overruled. Nobody escapes God's judgment by declining to acknowledge it, any more than a man escapes a court by refusing the summons.

For behold, I begin to work disaster at the city that is called by my name, and shall you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, for I am summoning a sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of hosts.'

Here is the logic of the whole chapter, and it is the argument from privilege running in the direction people least expect. God begins at the city that is called by my name. If he does not spare the place where he put his own name, on what basis would anyone else be spared?

Amos said it: You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you (Amos 3:2). Peter says it to the church: it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? (1 Pet 4:17).

Closeness to God is not immunity. It is responsibility, and it means the searchlight starts at home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–38 — The LORD Will Roar from on High
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD will roar from on high and shout like a man treading grapes against all the earth's inhabitants (v. 30), for the LORD has an indictment against the nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh (v. 31). Disaster goes from nation to nation (v. 32), and the slain will lie unburied from one end of the earth to the other (v. 33). Wail, you shepherds, for no refuge or escape remains (vv. 34-36), and the peaceful folds are devastated by his fierce anger (vv. 37-38).
verseByVerse.theology: The local catastrophe opens out into a universal one: God has a case against the whole world.

verseByVerse.quote: "You, therefore, shall prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: "'The LORD will roar from on high, and from his holy habitation utter his voice; he will roar mightily against his fold, and shout, like those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth. The clamor will resound to the ends of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against the nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh, and the wicked he will put to the sword, declares the LORD.' "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, disaster is going forth from nation to nation, and a great tempest is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth! "And those pierced by the LORD on that day shall extend from one end of the earth to the other. They shall not be lamented, or gathered, or buried; they shall be dung on the surface of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You, therefore, shall prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: "'The LORD will roar from on high, and from his holy habitation utter his voice; he will roar mightily against his fold, and shout, like those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth.

Two sounds. The first is a lion's roar, which is how prophets describe God going out to judgment. The second is stranger and more chilling: the shout of men treading grapes.

A winepress shout was a work song, the noise of a harvest celebration. God is pictured shouting it over the nations, and what is being crushed is not fruit. Revelation takes the same image to its end in the great winepress of the wrath of God.

Note also where he roars first: against his fold. Again, his own flock is where it begins.

The clamor will resound to the ends of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against the nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh, and the wicked he will put to the sword, declares the LORD.'

The legal word is used: God has an indictment, a case with charges. This is not rage; it is a court sitting, and the defendant is all flesh.

Everything local in the book — a small kingdom, a siege, a temple — opens here into something universal. The God of Judah is the judge of the world.

"Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, disaster is going forth from nation to nation, and a great tempest is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth!

Disaster spreads like weather, moving country to country. Anyone who has watched a crisis cross borders in a single year recognises the picture.

"And those pierced by the LORD on that day shall extend from one end of the earth to the other. They shall not be lamented, or gathered, or buried; they shall be dung on the surface of the ground.

The phrase from 8:2 and 16:4 returns, now on a global scale, and with the same three denials: no mourning, no gathering, no burial. This is what the Bible means when it refuses to make judgment sound tidy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Wail, you shepherds, and cry out, and roll in ashes, you lords of the flock, for the days of your slaughter and dispersion have come, and you shall fall like a choice vessel. No refuge will remain for the shepherds, nor escape for the lords of the flock. A voice—the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock! For the LORD is laying waste their pasture, and the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the LORD. Like a lion he has left his lair, for their land has become a waste because of the sword of the oppressor, and because of his fierce anger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Wail, you shepherds, and cry out, and roll in ashes, you lords of the flock, for the days of your slaughter and dispersion have come, and you shall fall like a choice vessel.

The shepherds are back — the leaders of chapter 23 — and now they are told to mourn for themselves. Roll in ashes is the most abject grief the culture had.

And the simile lands with the sound of the broken flask: you shall fall like a choice vessel. Not a cheap pot; a good one, the sort a household is proud of. It shatters exactly the same way.

No refuge will remain for the shepherds, nor escape for the lords of the flock.

Those who had refuges and escape routes — position, money, foreign contacts — find they have run out. The verse is blunt about what leadership cannot buy.

A voice—the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock! For the LORD is laying waste their pasture, and the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the LORD.

You can hear it before you see it: a voice, a cry, a wail. And what is destroyed is described with an aching phrase — the peaceful folds, the quiet places where sheep were safe.

Like a lion he has left his lair, for their land has become a waste because of the sword of the oppressor, and because of his fierce anger."

The chapter ends with the lion out of the thicket, as chapter 4 had it (4:7), and with two causes named in one breath: the sword of the oppressor, and his fierce anger. The human and the divine in the same event, which is how this whole book reads history.

And for the reader who has followed the cup around the nations, there is one more thing to say. The cup went to Jerusalem first, and the last of David's line to hold it did not stagger or refuse. He took it in a garden, prayed over it, and drank it down.

25.title: Seventy Years and the Cup of Wrath
25.overview:
In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Jeremiah sums up twenty-three years of preaching: the word came persistently, God persistently sent his prophets, the message was always to turn from evil and not serve other gods, and the response was that they did not listen, to their own harm (vv. 1-7).

So God will summon the tribes of the north and Nebuchadnezzar, whom he calls my servant, banishing the voices of mirth and marriage, the sound of the millstones and the light of the lamp; these nations will serve Babylon seventy years, after which Babylon itself will be punished and repaid according to its deeds (vv. 8-14).

Then the cup of the wine of wrath is put into Jeremiah's hand for all the nations. Jerusalem drinks first, then Egypt, the Philistine cities, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, the desert tribes, Elam and Media, and every kingdom on earth, with Babylon last (vv. 15-26). They must drink, and if they refuse they will drink anyway, for judgment begins at the city called by God's name (vv. 27-29).

Finally God roars from on high like a lion and shouts like a man treading grapes, bringing an indictment against all flesh; the slain will lie unburied from one end of the earth to the other, and the shepherds are told to wail, for no refuge remains (vv. 30-38).
25.theology:
Faithfulness, not visible response, is the measure of a ministry: twenty-three years summarised as unheard (v. 3). God's patience is measured in messengers persistently sent (v. 4).

God governs the empires that punish his people — Nebuchadnezzar is called my servant (v. 9) — and still holds them accountable for their own iniquity (vv. 12-14; Rom 2:6). His judgments are timed and limited: seventy years, read later by Daniel and the Chronicler (v. 11; Dan 9:2; 2 Chr 36:20-21).

The cup of wrath is a measured draught the nations must drink (vv. 15-28; Ps 75:8; Isa 51:17; Rev 14:10), and Christ asked for this cup in Gethsemane and drank it for his people (Matt 26:39). Judgment begins at the household of God (v. 29; Amos 3:2; 1 Pet 4:17): nearness to God is responsibility, not immunity.
25.examples:
Twenty-three years of work summed up in five words: you have not listened.

Judgment taking away the millstone at dawn and the lamp at night.

A pagan emperor called God's servant, and judged for how he served.

An exile with an expiry date, read by Daniel in a book.

Empires pictured as a drunk who cannot get up.

The cup handed round the nations, and drained in a garden.
